#5255. Stop Building AI Into Your Product. Let Your Customers Bring Their Own.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your B2B customers already pay for an AI assistant. “Bring your own agent” lets you plug into it instead of competing with it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past two years, almost every software company has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated. So we all did. Chat panels appeared in the corner of every dashboard. “Summarize with AI” buttons showed up next to every text field. Pricing pages grew a new line item for AI credits.

I run a company that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too. But somewhere along the way, I noticed something about our customers that changed how I think about the whole question.

If you sell to businesses, look at what your customers’ employees have open on their screens. Very often it’s a corporate Claude or ChatGPT subscription, or Microsoft 365 Copilot bundled into the Office licenses the company was paying for anyway. Someone in IT or finance evaluated it, signed a contract, went through a security review and rolled it out.

That assistant is becoming the company’s “at-home AI.” It’s the one employees are trained on, the one legal has approved, and increasingly, the one that has context about the business: documents, email, meeting notes, internal wikis. Every company will have one eventually. Frankly, most already do.

Now imagine that same company uses eight or 10 business tools, and each of those vendors has bolted on its own AI assistant. Each one has a different interface, different limits and different data policies. None of them know what the others know. The help desk AI has no idea what was discussed in the CRM, and the CRM’s AI can’t see the project tracker.

That’s not a better workplace. It’s AI sprawl, and it’s the opposite of what the customer wants.

The alternative is simple: Instead of building an assistant into your product, make your product easy for the customer’s existing assistant to use. Let them bring their own agent.

If that phrase sounds familiar, it should. A decade ago, “bring your own device” (BYOD) changed how companies thought about laptops and phones. More recently, “bring your own key” (BYOK) let customers plug their own AI provider’s API key into software instead of paying the vendor for AI usage. Bring your own agent (BYOA) is the next step: The customer doesn’t just bring the key; they bring the whole assistant, with its context, its permissions and its security approvals already in place.

For the customer, the benefits are obvious. They use a tool they already pay for and already know. Their assistant can combine data from your product with everything else it has access to. Asking “which of our biggest accounts filed support tickets this week, and what did we promise them in the last renewal call?” only works if one assistant can see both the help desk and the meeting notes.

For the vendor, the benefits are less obvious but just as real.

You stay out of the token-reselling business: When you build AI features on top of a model provider, you’re effectively buying compute wholesale and reselling it. Your costs grow with usage, your margins depend on someone else’s pricing changes, and you end up designing credit systems and usage caps instead of building your actual product. With BYOA, the customer’s AI subscription covers the compute. Your product provides the data and the actions.

You stop competing with companies that spend billions on models: No software vendor of normal size is going to build a better general-purpose assistant than the frontier AI labs. Trying to match them feature for feature is a losing race. Being the best tool their assistant can connect to is a race you can actually win.

It clarifies product decisions: This one surprised me the most. Once you accept that the customer’s assistant will handle the conversation, the question shifts from “What AI features should we build?” to “What can our product do, and how cleanly can we expose it?” That’s a much healthier question. It pushes you to make your core functionality solid, well-structured and well-permissioned, which is good for every user, not just the ones using AI.

It’s a marketing channel, too: This is the least obvious benefit. AI clients now have their own connector directories, and there’s a growing number of independent MCP registries and listing sites. Getting listed puts your product in front of people at the exact moment they’re looking for tools to connect to their assistant. It’s a new distribution channel, it’s still relatively uncrowded, and it costs you nothing beyond the integration you were building anyway.

This doesn’t mean built-in AI has no place. Some features, such as automatic ticket categorization that runs in the background without anyone asking, make sense to keep inside the product. But the conversational assistant, the one people talk to, increasingly belongs to the customer, not to you.

The practical way to do this today is to implement an MCP server for your product. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets AI assistants discover and use tools in external applications. It’s supported by Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot Studio and a growing list of other clients. You describe what your product can do, such as search records, create items or update statuses, and any compatible assistant can use those actions on the user’s behalf, within that user’s existing permissions.

There are two common ways to ship an MCP server, and the choice matters more than it seems.

1. A hosted endpoint over HTTP: Your product exposes an MCP endpoint on its own servers, using the protocol’s streamable HTTP transport. The customer adds a URL to their assistant, signs in, and that’s it. Nothing gets installed. When you add new capabilities or fix a bug, every customer gets the update immediately, because there’s only one version: the one you’re running.

2. A local package. You publish a command-line tool or npm package that runs on the user’s machine and talks to your API. This was the common approach early on, and it still works for individual developers.

I strongly recommend the first option. We started with both at my company, and we’re now phasing out the local package. Each installed copy is a version you can’t update, and customers running old packages kept missing newer features.

But the bigger reason is security. Large organizations increasingly won’t allow third-party code to run on employee machines, and for good reason. The past couple of years have brought a steady stream of critical-severity vulnerabilities and software supply chain attacks, including compromised packages in the npm ecosystem itself. Asking a security team to approve a package that runs locally with access to company data is a hard sell. Asking them to approve an HTTPS endpoint on a vendor they’ve already vetted is a much easier conversation.

A hosted endpoint also fits how companies roll out AI. Organization-wide connectors in enterprise AI plans are typically set up once by an administrator and then made available to everyone. Support OAuth sign-in so each employee connects with their own account and permissions, and you’ve removed most of the friction.

It’s tempting to view the customer’s AI assistant as a competitor for attention. If people spend their day in Claude or Copilot, won’t they spend less time in your product?

Maybe. But they were going to use that assistant anyway. The real question is whether it can reach your product when they need it. If it can’t, you’re the tool that gets worked around. If it can, you’re part of how the company works.

B2B buyers don’t want another AI. They want the one they already have to work with everything else they pay for. Build for that.

Over the past two years, almost every software company has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated. So we all did. Chat panels appeared in the corner of every dashboard. “Summarize with AI” buttons showed up next to every text field. Pricing pages grew a new line item for AI credits.

I run a company that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too. But somewhere along the way, I noticed something about our customers that changed how I think about the whole question.

#5254. Can Institutions Secretly Buy Billions of XRP? Ripple Veteran Says It Is 'Not Impossible'

Ripple’s longtime CTO emeritus David Schwartz does not think institutions can privately snap up billions of XRP via dark pools without affecting the token’s price on public markets.

"I don't think so. Who are they buying the XRP from? Why wouldn't people generally want the price to rise when they buy? But it's not impossible," Schwartz wrote on X on Nov. 24.

This was in response to a question posed by an XRP community member wondering if private trading platforms might give institutions an advantage over retail investors.

Earlier in the conversation, Schwartz noted the pros and cons of dark pools for retail traders.

He mentioned one disadvantage: less efficient price discovery. Given that bids and offers are obscured, retail traders in public markets have less insight into other traders’ bids and ask prices.

If there is a large XRP holder who is already inclined to sell at the current price, an institution could arrange a private trade with this holder without needing to place a massive buy order on an exchange. They could execute the trade without driving the public price up as they buy.

However, will there be enough sellers interested in offloading billions of XRP like this? One might run out of sellers willing to sell at that price. So, the buyer might need to up the ante to find the next willing seller.

A dark pool can hide order size, but one still needs someone on the other side to execute that order.

Plus, a buyer will naturally prefer not to tip its hand while accumulating a position.

Schwartz left open the possibility of a private purchase at scale, but the possibility is rather low.

When asked why XRP Ledger developments were not doing anything for XRP’s price on Nov. 9, Schwartz pointed to the broader crypto market.

He also debunked the notion that Ripple had some secret plan it was not sharing with holders. The company regularly talks about its plans.

Schwartz also mentioned a practical benefit of XRP being worth more in the: a higher price could mean cheaper liquidity provision and less slippage (the difference between the expected price a trader pays and the price they actually pay).

At the same time, he was less convinced that demand for XRP to pay transaction fees could have a big impact on the price by itself.

#5253. Etzioni on AI: 18 ways to use AI this Thanksgiving

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:17 amNovember 25, 2026 at 10:16 am

Here are 18 creative ways to use AI this Thanksgiving. Some save you time in the kitchen or at the airport, and others aim to make the meal more fun. The don’ts at the end could save your turkey, and my very last suggestion is perhaps the best.

Flight delay forecasting. Apps like Flighty (start with free tier) use machine learning to predict whether your flight will leave on time and why it might not.

Cancellation playbook drafted in advance. Have the backup flights and a rebooking script ready ahead of time, so a cancellation means consulting your AI instead of starting from scratch.

Airport pickup routing. Five relatives land at different times at two airports, and AI works out who drives whom. It can even send a polite request on your behalf.

A personal travel agent. Vayo (free, private beta), a new Seattle startup co-founded by my friend Mike Fridgen, connects to your inbox and pulls in your flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. It keeps an eye on them for price drops and changes.

Oven Tetris. Give it your oven’s size, every dish’s temperature and the serving time. It works backward to a minute-by-minute schedule and flags the conflicts.

Decoding grandma’s recipe card. Photograph the card and have AI modernize it under one rule: it never invents quantities. “A pinch” stays “a pinch.” “un poco” or “ein bissl” may be translated, but not changed.

Reconstructing a lost dish. Several relatives describe a dish a late grandparent made. AI triangulates a recipe, you cook test versions, and the family votes on which one tastes right.

Pairing from the wines on hand. AI picks from bottles you actually own, and those brought over by guests, dish by dish, instead of a generic list. Last-minute fun!

Potluck dispatcher. One AI thread collects RSVPs and dish claims so you don’t end up with four green bean casseroles.

Trivia built from your own family’s facts. ChatGPT can now run it as a playable game, with answer buttons and a running score inside the conversation.

AI-prepped grandparent interview. Feed the AI what you already know and have it draft questions about the gaps. Record it, and afterward AI turns the transcript into a short illustrated booklet that’s in the mail by Christmas.

Angry Uncle rehearsal. Karin Tamerius, a political psychiatrist, built the Angry Uncle Bot, and it still runs in ChatGPT. A coach asks for your issue and your stance. You set the uncle’s temper from Annoyed to Apoplectic and choose whether he’s drunk or sober, and the coach critiques each reply before he answers.

Live interpreter for multilingual families. Put ChatGPT’s voice mode (paid plans) in the middle of the table so the great-aunt who only speaks Hebrew or Spanish is part of the conversation instead of watching it.

Friday leftover remix. Photograph the fridge and get a menu that makes Friday’s leftovers feel like a new meal.

Specific thank-you notes. Each note names what that person actually brought or said.

Photo triage. AI picks the best 20 of 400 photos and captions them in the family’s inside-joke voice.

“We missed you” letter for someone who wasn’t at the table. AI drafts it from the stories told at dinner.

Black Friday skeptic. Before you buy, check Google’s price insights, which tells you whether a price is high, low or typical for the past three months. Last year, 36% of Black Friday items showed no savings over their prices a few weeks earlier. Better yet, set a price track and let Google’s agent buy the item at eligible U.S. stores when it hits your number, after you confirm.

I consider myself an OG Black Friday skeptic. Back in 2011, I told the New York Times (gift link) that after crunching the price data at my startup Decide.com, the lowest electronics prices usually came in early December, not on Black Friday.

Don’t trust an AI turkey recipe on its own. Back in 2022, when the New York Times cooked a Thanksgiving from GPT-3 recipes, the turkey recipe called for one garlic clove for a 12-pound bird and no butter or oil. It came out dry and flavorless.

Don’t take a chatbot’s word on an airline’s rules. Air Canada’s chatbot told a grieving passenger he could claim a bereavement discount after he flew. The real policy said no, and he had to take the airline to a tribunal to collect $812 (Canadian). Check the airline’s own policy page, and screenshot what the bot tells you.

Don’t click on the deal of the century. Scammers now use AI to make fake shopping sites look legitimate, and the number of fake sites jumped 250% last holiday season, according to NordVPN. Type the retailer’s address yourself.

Don’t try to win the family argument with AI-fetched facts. Even the creator of Angry Uncle Bot says that bombarding your uncle with facts only makes him angrier. Ask questions and listen instead.

Here’s another option: give technology a rest.

Unplug from your devices and from AI, and have an AI-free, 100% human Thanksgiving.

#5252. A Bigger Business Isn’t Automatically a Better One. Here’s What to Ask Before Scaling.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Scaling a business isn’t just about hiring more people and increasing revenue. Growth brings new management challenges, operational complexity and the risk of losing sight of customers.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve spent 13 years building a business. It’s long enough to figure out what works, and definitely long enough to get a lot of things wrong. When we were five people in a 300-square-foot office, our team tripled in size in a year. Our client base and revenue grew just as quickly. At some point, I genuinely started to believe we were the gods of consulting. As it turned out, we were simply very good at running a small company.

That is one of the lovely things about early success. It gives you confidence and the impression that you have figured out the whole business. Now that I’ve had time to reflect, I see that the first lesson of scaling is that success at one stage doesn’t automatically prepare you for the next.

If a team of five can become 10 by working harder and talking more, it’s tempting to assume that 10 can become 50 the same way. But growth is not multiplication. A company of eight people and a company of 30 are not the same business at different sizes. They are two different organizations that require two different ways of managing.

In its early days, a small company can get by on instinct, proximity and a good deal of improvisation just because, as a founder, you are involved in nearly everything. You know the clients, notice the work, answer questions and make decisions often before anyone has had time to schedule a meeting about them.

For me, the hardest part wasn’t letting go of tasks. It was realizing that the quality of my business now depended on decisions I wasn’t making, and sometimes didn’t even know were being made.

This is a transition I didn’t handle perfectly. One of my wrong calls was appointing people to management roles because they were excellent specialists. It seemed reasonable at the time, but expertise in consulting doesn’t automatically equip someone to lead a team or resolve a conflict. The difference becomes significant when the business depends on managers to preserve quality without the founder standing nearby.

I am convinced that a company must become less dependent on its founder at precisely the moment the founder may feel most protective of it. That requires more than delegating tasks. I’d say develop leaders who can exercise judgment, establish standards that don’t live solely in the founder’s memory and distribute authority with enough clarity. Without it, founders often remain the final decision-makers, even after building several layers of management.

If you recognize your business in this stage of growth, Ichak Adizes’s model of the company life cycle offers a useful way to understand this transition. The entrepreneurial “Go-Go” stage, with its energy and instinct for opportunity, eventually gives way to “Adolescence,” when informal habits must yield to professional management and clearer authority.

These growing pains don’t necessarily mean you’re running a bad business. On the contrary, they may simply mean you’ve outgrown the way you used to run it. This model gives founders a way to understand why the habits that helped a young company move quickly may no longer serve the organization as it grows.

One of the easiest traps to fall into when scaling is that you can become so busy building the company that you forget who you’re building it for. You can look at your dashboard, see rising revenue and new sign-ups, and think you’re winning. Meanwhile, right under your nose, the quality your loyal clients are getting is quietly tanking.

It’s incredibly easy to lose sight of the customer when your calendar is consumed by recruitment and endless alignments. You end up stuck in back-to-back meetings talking about structure, while your actual clients are dealing with junior staff who don’t fully understand their business yet.

Ask yourself, when was the last time you personally spoke to a client not to sell them something, but to understand whether your company is still delivering the value they expect?

As a business grows, the cost of complexity grows with it. More employees mean more coordination, more management responsibilities and more opportunities for processes to break down. Before committing to another expansion push, it’s worth looking at the reality of the market.

OECD figures show that among SMEs with 10 to 249 employees, 8% to 14% qualified as employment scalers in 2020, while 12% to 24% qualified as turnover scalers. The OECD also found that scalers were, on average, 20% more productive than other SMEs before their high-growth phase, with that advantage rising to 35% after three years.

What this reinforces for me is that expansion should never be an automatic next step. I try to keep that question front and center; otherwise, you can become so absorbed in perfecting the company’s internal structure that you stop thinking about the actual person using your product.

So before the next growth effort, make sure you do not scale chaos:

Not every business needs to become bigger. Sometimes scaling creates value. Sometimes it simply creates overhead. More employees do not automatically mean more success. More markets do not automatically mean more opportunities. And higher revenue does not necessarily mean a healthier business.

In specialist consulting, a focused team of 10 can be more profitable and resilient than an organization of 50. In fintech, entering another country may be strategically sound, or it may add cost and complexity without improving the customer proposition.

When we were five people in that small office, I thought learning to make money meant I knew how to build a big business. It took me 13 years to realize that building a bigger company and building a better company are not the same thing.

I’ve spent 13 years building a business. It’s long enough to figure out what works, and definitely long enough to get a lot of things wrong. When we were five people in a 300-square-foot office, our team tripled in size in a year. Our client base and revenue grew just as quickly. At some point, I genuinely started to believe we were the gods of consulting. As it turned out, we were simply very good at running a small company.

That is one of the lovely things about early success. It gives you confidence and the impression that you have figured out the whole business. Now that I’ve had time to reflect, I see that the first lesson of scaling is that success at one stage doesn’t automatically prepare you for the next.

If a team of five can become 10 by working harder and talking more, it’s tempting to assume that 10 can become 50 the same way. But growth is not multiplication. A company of eight people and a company of 30 are not the same business at different sizes. They are two different organizations that require two different ways of managing.

#5251. Ethereum Foundation Sounds Alarm Over AI Threats

The Ethereum Foundation has been working for years to secure the network against a future in which quantum computing breaks the cryptography underpinning Ethereum, but it is now facing a new and more immediate concern around artificial intelligence.

AI is identifying bugs in live software more quickly than human reviewers can keep up with, and the Ethereum Foundation has now doubled the size of its protocol security team, according to a recent announcement.

As Kev Wedderburn wrote in a post from Devcon, AI models are now identifying thousands of bugs in the Linux kernel, one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world.

For Ethereum developers, the immediate challenge is ensuring that bugs are not present in their software before an upgrade.

The longer-term challenge is mathematical. Ethereum uses digital signatures to identify who can spend funds and which validators have approved the state of the chain.

Wedderburn says that AI's advances in analyzing decades-old algorithms raise questions about the mathematical assumptions underlying those signatures that researchers should consider.

It is not clear whether AI could break Ethereum's existing cryptography. However,  the Ethereum Foundation wants work on new cryptography to be underway.

After more than a year of considering various signature schemes, the Ethereum Foundation has decided to replace elliptic-curve signatures with hash-based cryptography.

The argument is that Ethereum already relies on cryptographic hash security, and by using hashes for signatures too, it can remove an additional assumption about the difficulty of solving mathematical problems associated with elliptic curves.

The proposal affects three areas of Ethereum.

It would see validators use hash-based keys for their signatures, which in turn changes how block finality is determined on the network.

Wallet developers would need to provide users with a way to transition their accounts to hash-based signatures.

And Ethereum's change to the cryptography used for commitments to data (blobs) that rollups publish to the network would require adjustments from rollups too.

One challenge is the size of the signatures. Hash-based signatures are much larger, so developers need to consider how that affects the hardware needed to run a node at home.

Staking pools and multisig wallets would need adjustments too. So would smart contracts that rely on existing cryptography.

There will also be a need to adjust tools that rely on the signature scheme currently used by Ethereum validators (BLS).

#5250. FCC clears SpaceX to put up to a million satellites in orbit for Starmind data center network

by Alan Boyle on Nov 25, 2026 at 4:46 pmNovember 25, 2026 at 4:46 pm

The Federal Communications Commission has authorized SpaceX to send up to a million satellites into orbit for its Starmind data-processing network.

In a news release, the FCC touted today’s decision as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space” and echoed the high-flown language that SpaceX used to describe the network in its application 10 months ago.

“It promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization — one that can harness the full power of the sun,” the agency said.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the plan “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Carr signaled that he was all in on the Trump administration’s support for rapid data center expansion, despite a growing backlash that figured in this month’s midterm elections. He said that “compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership” in artificial intelligence.

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” Carr said.

In a post to X, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk told Carr that his praise was “much appreciated.”

“This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk said.

Proponents of solar-powered orbital data centers say such constellations will address the top concerns about terrestrial data centers, including land use, power consumption and water requirements for cooling. Critics point to the engineering challenges, including concerns about cooling the satellites, managing space traffic and dealing with orbital debris.

In approving SpaceX’s application, the FCC rejected opposition from Amazon and Viasat, as well as from the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about the constellation’s impact on the night sky. The AAS said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

The FCC attached several conditions to its authorization, including requirements for communications backups, regular updates and a detailed plan for orbital debris mitigation.

SpaceX was cleared to operate its satellites at orbits ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (310 to 623 miles) in altitude. The first satellite is to be put into operation no later than 2033, and the FCC calls for the full constellation to be operating by 2040.

In August, SpaceX announced that it was partnering with Nvidia to design the compute payload for the Starmind AI1 satellite. “Each of the Starmind satellites will include Nvidia Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs for datacenter-class space compute,” SpaceX said at the time.

SpaceX’s facility in Redmond, Wash., makes the satellites for the Starlink telecommunications network — but in a filing related to this year’s initial public offering, SpaceX said its operation in Bastrop, Texas, would be put in charge of producing AI compute satellites.

The FCC said it is continuing to review additional orbital data center proposals and intends to issue decisions on each proposal “according to the agency’s regular procedures.”

XRP has printed a substantial exchange outflow, with 270 million XRP moving out of Uphold in 24 hours. That's three transfers of 90 million XRP each. The transfers raise more questions about what large holders are doing while XRP struggles below $1.

The three transfers went to rP2Sxx…jzmV, rhDoUm…LVNk and rKB4EP…YUs3. In total, 78 transfers crossed the 1 million XRP threshold, moving 523 million XRP. Of the transfers tracked, 31 worth a combined 75.8 million XRP were movements between wallets belonging to the same owners. Taking those out gives us a clearer picture of transfers to outside wallets.

More XRP was removed from known exchange wallets than added to them. Outflows reached 456.2 million XRP, while inflows sat at 181.7 million XRP. Uphold led with a net outflow of 269.1 million XRP. Robinhood saw the largest net inflow at 13.5 million XRP.

Inflows and outflows can reflect usual trading and investment activities, including investors moving funds into self-custody. It's important to keep in mind that if those tokens stay off exchanges, there could be less XRP readily available for sale. It's not clear whether there's any accumulation here. The next thing to watch is whether the funds stay in those wallets or move back to an exchange.

XRP was trading at $0.9376, up 1.15% over 24 hours. It traded as low as $0.9124 and as high as $1.024 in that window. XRP is still below all the major moving averages on the daily chart. The downtrend that took hold in November is still in place. RSI is borderline oversold, so selling pressure might be fading. A sustained recovery is yet to come.

On November 22, the XRP Ledger recorded 2.8 million transactions and 3,833 new wallets. Payment volume reached 997.2 million XRP, while active accounts sat at 41,800. The network activity is still non-zero, though the transaction count is declining. The performance of XRP leaves a lot to be desired. The confirmation of a market recovery would only come if we witness stronger buying in the foreseeable future.

#5247. ‘Aether & Iron’: Seattle-area indie game studio builds a noir detective RPG in the sky

by Thomas Wilde on Nov 26, 2026 at 8:51 amNovember 26, 2026 at 8:51 am

Some video games exist at the confluence point between a surprising number of genres, which can make them difficult to explain to people who aren’t hip-deep in the hobby. That’s why several of the most popular categories are currently nicknamed after the most visible games in them, such as the “Metroidvania” or “Soulslike.” Sure, this isn’t anywhere near the biggest problem in the video game industry at the moment, but we’re going to have to figure this out sooner or later.

Aether & Iron, created by the Issaquah, Wash.-based developer Seismic Squirrel, with co-developer Chaos Theory Games, is at one of those weird genre points. It’s described by its developers as a “narrative RPG,” which works well enough, but that also doesn’t exactly say that much.

It’s worth saying up front that Aether & Iron is on a slow boil. It’s a 30-hour game that unfolds at a careful pace, building out an elaborate science-fiction setting from first principles. If you’re looking for fast thrills, it’s not the experience for you. Instead, think of it like a long novel with points of potential failure, where every opportunity for interactivity is also a chance for you to take its story in a different direction.

Aether & Iron is set in an alternate universe where a strange substance called aether was found beneath Manhattan in 1871. Sixty-seven years later, the study and exploitation of aether has become its own branch of science, which led to a great technological leap forward. Much of New York has been transformed into a three-tiered flying city, split between the Lowers, the Uppers and the Heights. The higher a neighborhood flies, the higher its society.

You enter the story in 1938 in the role of Gia Randazzo, a smuggler from the Lowers who’s hit hard times. She’s so desperate for work that she takes a job she shouldn’t, as a driver and bodyguard for a young scientist from the Heights named Eleanor Reinhardt. It should be a milk run, but Dr. Reinhardt has enemies she doesn’t know about.

In short order, an assassin tries to kill them both, someone steals Gia’s car, and she and Dr. Reinhardt end up stuck together in the worst parts of the Lowers. With no money, a loaner vehicle and few friends left, Gia has to figure out who wants Dr. Reinhardt dead and why. That puts her on a collision course with a revolutionary movement, several of New York’s power brokers and a conspiracy that could knock the city back out of the sky.

You could call Aether & Iron something like “airship noir.” Despite its science-fiction trappings, it’s a dark detective novel at heart. Yes, humanity’s built up into the sky, but the street is always the street. Mickey Spillane meets William Gibson.

During dialogue and investigation sequences, Aether & Iron uses a pair of virtual six-sided dice to determine whether you succeed or fail at a given task. As you get further into the game, you can acquire items that let you reroll those dice on a failed check.

More importantly, you earn experience points for accomplishments and victories, which grant you skill points that can be spent in one of nine categories. You can customize Gia to follow several distinct character tracks, such as a detective, a back-alley brawler or a fast-talking con woman. That influences the path you take through the game and the options that become available to you.

No matter how you choose to play Gia, you can’t always avoid a fight. All the combat in Aether & Iron takes place behind the wheel, with Gia and her crew driving customized vehicles. You can acquire a whole fleet of cars and trucks, then kit them out with special weapons, utility devices, armored plates and matching paint jobs.

Each fight consists of a turn-based tactical battle through the streets in and around New York. In addition to simply shooting up an enemy, you can sideswipe them to force them off the road or into other cars.

Many of the city’s thoroughfares are falling apart or prone to sudden lane changes, so most fights will have their own set of additional hazards. Fortunately, they’re as dangerous to your enemies as they are to you, so you can exploit the road hazards if you think fast enough.

If I had to point at one problem I’ve got with Aether & Iron, it might be that the combat has a couple of unlabeled difficulty curves. Specifically, a few fights are built around specific types of damage to such a degree that the only real way past them is to reload an old save and modify all my vehicles for that particular encounter.

If you like the idea of constantly tweaking your vehicle collection for specific combat purposes, like heat shielding or knockback resistance, you’ll have some fun here. If you’re like me and you tend to rely on set-and-forget general-purpose builds, you’ll run into some roadblocks.

Other than that, you might know already whether or not you want to check it out. There’s a lot of care and art in Aether & Iron, mixed with a unique science-fiction setting that isn’t quite like anything else in video games at the moment.

Aether & Iron is currently available for PC and Mac via Steam for $24.99. Seismic Squirrel plans to release the game for PlayStation and Xbox in 2027.

#5246. I Run a Marketing Agency. Here’s Where Founders Go Wrong When They Copy Big Brands.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Chasing a competitor’s ad campaign skips the work that actually made it succeed: getting the positioning, messaging and channels right first.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every founder has stared at an industry leader’s ad campaign and thought, “That’s what we need.” The reasoning feels sound. That brand is growing; that brand made this ad; therefore, the ad must be why it’s growing. So the founder hires a director who can shoot something similarly polished, picks the same three platforms and waits for the same results.

The results rarely come, and budget was never the missing ingredient. The real problem sits earlier than that. Founders studying a category leader almost always study the wrong version of them. They look at the leader today, serving tens of millions of users with broad, generic messaging built to resonate with every persona in the market at once, and they try to mimic that. But the leader didn’t start there. Facebook, for example, launched as an invitation-only network open only to students with a university email address, and that scarcity created a fear of missing out among a small, sharply defined first audience. The broad, everyone-welcome version came only after that early foothold was won. Reverse engineering a category leader is a smart move. Reverse engineering the wrong point in their timeline isn’t.

In my years running a mobile-first agency, I’ve sat across the table from founders trying to catch up to them, and the pattern is consistent. The brands that dominate their categories got four fundamentals right before they ever turned on an ad, and they keep getting them right long after the launch buzz fades. Positioning, messaging, creative and channel selection aren’t separate skills. They’re a sequence, and skipping ahead is what sinks most growth plans.

Before you write a single line of copy, you need a clear answer to why someone should choose you over every other option competing for their attention. Category leaders have this answer nailed down internally long before the market ever sees a campaign. It shows up in how the sales team talks, how the product is built and how customer support responds to complaints.

Picture a two-person software startup that spends three months redesigning its logo and website before ever testing whether customers understood the old positioning in the first place. That’s a common trap. If your team can’t state in one sentence why you exist and who you exist for, no amount of creative or clever channel selection will fix that gap. You’ll just be spending money to advertise confusion, and confused customers don’t convert. They scroll past.

A tagline is not messaging. Messaging is the full set of arguments your business makes for itself, and it needs to hold up against the actual objections your customers raise, not the scenarios your team imagined in a conference room. I’ve watched founders workshop language for weeks that sounds impressive internally and falls flat the moment a real prospect asks “why should I care.”

Test your messaging against actual sales conversations and actual customer support tickets before you scale it into ads. If your support team fields the same three questions every week, your messaging should already answer them before the customer asks. That’s not a nice-to-have. That’s the whole job of messaging, and category leaders treat it that way.

Here’s where founders lose the most time and money. A founder decides the business needs to be on TikTok, or that it needs video ads like a competitor’s, and treats the channel itself as the strategy. It isn’t. Channel selection should follow directly from where your positioning and messaging already resonate.

If you’re running a mobile app, this matters even more, because your app is competing for attention before a single paid ad ever runs. Your app store listing, your screenshots and the keywords you rank for are doing real marketing work the moment someone searches your category. That work only succeeds if the positioning underneath it is already solid. A founder who spends on paid user acquisition while ignoring app store optimization is filling a bucket with a hole in the bottom. Creative is the outfit. Strategy is the body wearing it. Founders who obsess over the outfit while ignoring the body end up with beautiful ads that don’t convert, because the fundamentals underneath were never built.

The uncomfortable truth is that category leaders aren’t smarter than you, and they don’t have some proprietary growth hack you’re missing. What they have is discipline, applied differently at different stages. They revisit their positioning as the market shifts. They retest their messaging as customer objections evolve. They treat channel selection as a live decision rather than a one-time setup.

A bigger spend buys reach. It doesn’t buy relevance, and reach without relevance is just an expensive way to be ignored. Massive brand growth comes from executing the fundamentals better than the competition, not from outspending it. But the fundamentals themselves change shape as you grow. A leader with millions of users has to speak to the common ground of every persona in their market, because that breadth is what their size demands. A founder without product market fit yet who tries to sound that broad from day one will resonate with none of those personas, because broad messaging is a privilege of scale, not a starting strategy.

Find the audience with the most acute version of the problem you solve. Win them completely before you widen the aperture. That’s the same path the leader you’re studying took before anyone called them a leader. Get your positioning right for the size you actually are and build messaging that survives real customer conversations. Starting early only gives you more time to refine and improve, and the founders who understand which stage they’re in will be the ones the next generation studies.

Every founder has stared at an industry leader’s ad campaign and thought, “That’s what we need.” The reasoning feels sound. That brand is growing; that brand made this ad; therefore, the ad must be why it’s growing. So the founder hires a director who can shoot something similarly polished, picks the same three platforms and waits for the same results.

The results rarely come, and budget was never the missing ingredient. The real problem sits earlier than that. Founders studying a category leader almost always study the wrong version of them. They look at the leader today, serving tens of millions of users with broad, generic messaging built to resonate with every persona in the market at once, and they try to mimic that. But the leader didn’t start there. Facebook, for example, launched as an invitation-only network open only to students with a university email address, and that scarcity created a fear of missing out among a small, sharply defined first audience. The broad, everyone-welcome version came only after that early foothold was won. Reverse engineering a category leader is a smart move. Reverse engineering the wrong point in their timeline isn’t.

In my years running a mobile-first agency, I’ve sat across the table from founders trying to catch up to them, and the pattern is consistent. The brands that dominate their categories got four fundamentals right before they ever turned on an ad, and they keep getting them right long after the launch buzz fades. Positioning, messaging, creative and channel selection aren’t separate skills. They’re a sequence, and skipping ahead is what sinks most growth plans.

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Shiba Inu (SHIB) community members have launched a new block explorer for Shibarium, the layer-2 network of the SHIB ecosystem, and Shiba Inu lead Shytoshi Kusama has remained silent on X since May.

Shiba Inu community veteran Mazrael announced the new explorer, scan.shibfun.app, in an X post. "Shibarium has a new block explorer," he wrote. According to Mazrael, the explorer was "built by the community, powered by ShibWatch, dressed in the Eternity Hub look."

The launch comes as SHIB trades near its lowest levels in years. In November, the price of SHIB fell as low as $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021, and on Nov. 22, the token traded at around $0.00000362, according to CoinMarketCap.

According to the post, users can type a .shib name in the search bar and land on the wallet linked to it, and the explorer also shows new Shiboshis from Shibarium every day. For developers, Mazrael listed contract verification, read and write functions for contracts, the activity of ERC-4337 smart wallets, and a free API, which he described as "Etherscan-style too." Method names are decoded as well, and in Mazrael's words, there are "no more mystery 0x codes." The explorer also has a DApps page with Shibarium games and apps, and a button that adds Shibarium to a wallet in one click.

The work on the explorer is not finished yet. "Live blocks are complete now, and older history indexing," Mazrael wrote. On Tuesday, the explorer itself showed that 3% of Shibarium blocks had been indexed, and a notice on the site said that some of the counts may be inaccurate. Mazrael added that the new explorer can be found on Shib.io under ShibWatch.

Shytoshi Kusama's last post or interaction on X dates back to May 13, 2026. In September, Kusama changed his X bio to "Polish" and his location to "Close," and he has not explained the meaning of either word. The official Shibarium account on X has not posted since July 13, 2026.

Still, Shibarium updates kept coming from community members. In October, Mazrael said that CreateX, a standard factory for deploying contracts at the same address on different chains, went live on Shibarium. According to Mazrael, all 12 Safe v1.4.1 contracts were deployed to their canonical addresses through the Safe Singleton Factory, and x402 went live too, so AI agents can now pay in SHIB, TREAT and wrapped BONE.

In September 2025, attackers exploited the Shibarium bridge and withdrew about $2.4 million worth of assets from it.

According to Shibariumscan, Shibarium processed 546 transactions in a single day in late November, and on Oct. 31, the daily number of transactions on the network was 6,370. Since its launch in August 2023, Shibarium has processed more than 1.5 billion transactions in total.

At the same time, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million on Nov. 17, according to Etherscan.

Will Crypto Recover? Everyone is wondering this right now after the entire crypto market surged around +2% overnight. An Optimistic Look After Bitcoin’s Rebound Above $ 60,000.

The cryptocurrency market delivered a welcome dose of relief over the past 24 hours. Bitcoin reclaimed the $60,000 level, rising roughly 2.5–3.5% to trade between $60,400 and $60,800, while the broader market advanced in tandem.

Ethereum climbed to the $1,690–$1,710 range, XRP advanced toward $0.95–$0.96, and total crypto market capitalization pushed higher toward $2.15–$2.16 trillion.

After weeks of heavy selling and extreme fear, the bounce has sparked renewed discussion about whether this could mark the early stages of a more sustained recovery heading into 2027.

Prices became deeply oversold after Bitcoin’s slide toward the mid-$50,000s earlier in the week, with short-term RSI readings hitting extreme lows that historically attract dip-buyers and mean-reversion algorithms.

Forced short covering amplified the move higher as leveraged bearish positions were liquidated. A concurrent recovery in technology and AI-related equities improved broader risk appetite, and crypto’s high correlation with those sectors helped lift digital assets.

Thin holiday trading volumes around Thanksgiving also magnified price swings. On the policy front, progress on a U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill that cleared a House committee provided a modest sentiment boost, reminding participants that longer-term institutional and governmental interest has not vanished.

XRP's Long Wait Could Finally Pay OffTokentus Investment CEO Oliver Michel expects $XRP (@XRP) to rally around February or March.He believes the next bullish phase could bring a major price peak. Michel says he could sell all his XRP holdings at that point.He previously… pic.twitter.com/MTq8iBJan3

Its ability to hold above $60,000 after testing lower support is constructive in the short term. While November has seen record ETF outflows exceeding $5 billion, the latest rebound shows that demand can still emerge at discounted levels.

Looking further ahead, the case for recovery into 2027 rests on several structural factors. Crypto markets have repeatedly shown resilience after deep corrections, often bottoming when sentiment reaches extreme fear, as in recent weeks.

Persistent institutional infrastructure, including spot ETFs, corporate treasury strategies, and ongoing development in tokenization and payments, provides a foundation for renewed capital inflows once macroeconomic conditions stabilize.

Policy developments, such as clearer regulatory frameworks or expanded strategic reserve discussions, could act as positive catalysts. One example is the US Bitcoin Strategic Reserve Bill, which was recently cleared and is now headed to the House.

Historically, post-halving cycles and periods of oversold conditions have preceded stronger multi-month advances, and many participants view current levels as a potential accumulation zone rather than the start of a prolonged bear market.

Of course, risks remain. Continued heavy ETF outflows, sticky inflation data, or a shift toward tighter monetary policy could pressure prices again.

Yet the speed with which buyers stepped in during the latest dip suggests underlying demand remains. If Bitcoin can build a series of higher lows and reclaim key moving averages, confidence is likely to improve across the board.

In short, while one rebound does not confirm a full bull market, the past 24 hours offer encouraging signs that selling pressure may be exhausting itself.

Combined with oversold technicals, short covering, supportive equity moves, and longer-term policy and institutional tailwinds, crypto has a credible path to recover more meaningfully through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027.

For now, the market has shown it can still bounce, and that alone is a constructive first step. However, green weekly closes across the major cap tokens are the next step in seeing whether this rally has any legs.

#5243. Startup Spotlight: Aventide builds AI client management software for consultants and coaches

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 27, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 25, 2026 at 2:33 pm

Christian Quiver and Eric Baxter met in a grocery store parking lot, introduced by their wives. Quiver needed a designer for a project, so the two swapped numbers and agreed to try working together for 90 days. Four years later, they’re building a startup together in the Columbia River Gorge.

Their startup, Aventide, opened to the public on Oct. 29. It’s AI-powered software for consultants, coaches and others who sell their expertise one client at a time. Aventide drafts proposals, invoices and follow-ups, but nothing goes to a client until the owner approves it.

Eric Baxter, CDO, and Christian Quiver, CEO, Founder

The name blends “abhainn,” the Irish Gaelic word for river, with “tide,” for the spot where a river meets the sea and where towns and ports have long grown up.

Quiver, the CEO, lives in White Salmon, Wash., and spent more than five years at Amazon. He led go-to-market for the in-store experience as Amazon’s device stores grew from two locations to 50. Baxter is chief design officer and lives in nearby Trout Lake. He spent 25 years in product design, including nearly seven years leading user experience at Welocalize, whose clients included Amazon, Google and Apple.

The idea started in 2025 with a question from Baxter’s wife: Which part of his decades of designing products for other people actually brought him joy? His answer was helping people, especially those pushed out by AI-era layoffs who were trying to start something of their own. Quiver bought in that October.

The pair spent more than six months testing with three groups of business owners in the Gorge, including at a demo day in June with the Mid-Columbia Innovation Hub. They kept meeting people who live in small towns and sell their expertise to companies in Seattle or Portland. “A consultant in a small town can land a corporate client,” Quiver said in an email.

The two-person company is bootstrapped and says 81 people are using Aventide so far. After a 14-day free trial, plans cost $39 or $99 a month. Aventide also publishes estimates of the electricity and water behind everyday tasks in the app. Quiver says the figures could be off by a factor of two either way. “If you ask what it costs in electricity and water to use our product, you get a straight answer,” he said.

We caught up with Quiver for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch?

Aventide is an AI-native client management platform for people paid by the session, project or event. It replaces separate booking, proposal, contract, portal and invoice apps, and runs more than one business from one login.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

Tool fragmentation in small client businesses, and the fact that the owner ends up being the human glue holding all of it together.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

That the barrier isn’t price or features. People don’t have time to switch systems, and many aren’t comfortable with their own software stack. So we onboard anyone who wants it one-on-one.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

Everything. It has fundamentally changed what a small team can build and run. We have always worked as experience builders first, and AI lets a team of two think bigger, test faster, and deliver a world-class product that would have taken what seems like 100-200 people just a year or two ago. It cuts our time from idea to execution by at least 50x.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

People hear “AI for small business” and picture a chat box taped onto legacy software. Instead of making you click through old CRM menus with a writing bot on the side, Aventide wires AI directly into your bookings, contracts, portals, and payments so you just say it, review it and approve.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Choosing which problem we wanted to solve. Our original mission was far too vague to build. We set out to help people through the AI era, but the interviews and prototypes kept landing on client services. Following that meant narrowing a big mission into one product for one kind of owner.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Think bigger, and focus on the whole experience you want to create. Outside of a few rare cases, narrow single-purpose tools are old hat now because nobody wants another tab to manage. The future belongs to software where someone can say, “This is my one tool for this category of my life.

50,000 human-scale businesses use Aventide to own their client relationships directly, keeping more money in small businesses and giving more time back to the people running them.

#5242. Flop Labs Pushes Back Testnet Launch Amid Final Preparations

Flop Labs has announced a minor delay to the launch of its public testnet, pushing back from its previous goal of 15:00 (UTC+8) on November 24.

It's unclear what the reason for the delay is, although the team does expect to launch the testnet before 18:00 (UTC+8) the same day.

Possible reasons for the delay could include conducting final checks, calibrating nodes, validator onboarding, load testing, etc. (although Flop Labs has not confirmed any of these to be the reason for the delay).

It does not appear that Flop Labs has any plans to move the testnet launch to another day.

Flop Labs is building FLOP Network, a blockchain serving as a settlement layer for what it calls the "agentic economy". This would enable AI agents to make payments for computation (e.g. model inference) and memory services, and provide rewards to GPU miners that contribute their computational power to fulfill these requests.

Computation is verified via Flop Labs' "Proof of Useful Inference", which entails miners providing evidence that they've carried out the desired AI computation, and validators checking this evidence.

Why does this matter? FLOP Network would enable agents to make payments for computation, memory, etc. Flop Labs' main competitors include Akash Network and io.net (both of which facilitate access to compute/gpu resources in a decentralized manner), as well as Render Network (which started out facilitating decentralized graphics rendering but has since expanded into AI/compute more broadly).

While Flop Labs' competitors also facilitate access to compute, Flop Labs' main differentiating factor appears to be its focus on facilitating agent-to-agent commerce and computation-verification.

Flop Labs is led by Arthur Hayes, co-founder of crypto exchange BitMEX and current chief investment officer at Maelstrom. The rest of Flop Labs' team includes Sergey Vidyuk (ex-Deutsche Bank/BitMEX) as CTO, and Shu Duan (with experience in investment banking and crypto asset management) as chief strategy officer.

The testnet would be an opportunity to see if Flop Labs can successfully build out its envisioned agentic economy.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 27, 2026 at 8:30 amNovember 27, 2026 at 8:30 am

Jeremy Sanford can’t control the weather that will hit ski resorts this winter, but he hopes his new app can at least tell you whether it’s worth loading up the car — or calling in sick.

Sanford, a senior product designer at Microsoft who grew up on the Eastside and has been skiing and snowboarding since he was a kid, has been building Pow Pow on nights and weekends, using “vibe coding” and Claude to do the work he couldn’t do himself.

The free app for iPhone and Android combines forecast data and readings from mountain snow sensors into snow reports for more than 200 resorts, from Snoqualmie Pass to Niseko, Japan.

Each resort gets a 1–5 “Pow Rating,” where a 5 means call in sick, and a blunt one-liner that says whether it really dumped overnight or your powder day is about to turn to rain.

For Sanford, the stakes come with a full car. He has two kids, ages 4 and 7, whom he is teaching to ski.

“I gotta load up the car with the kids and all the gear,” he said. “Is it just gonna be kind of crappy conditions when we get up there?”

He said none of the resort or weather apps he used gave him exactly what he wanted, and he didn’t fully trust the resorts’ numbers.

“You kind of got to take them with a grain of salt, because I feel like they inflate the numbers a little bit,” he said.

With Pow Pow, the aim is “an honest representation of what the conditions are actually like,” Sanford said. For the details, a section called “Nerd stuff” charts snowfall, base depth, snow quality, snow line, wind and UV.

“It’s got six inches of snow overnight, but what else is going on?” he said. “Oh, it’s maybe super wet up there now, and it’s supposed to be raining this afternoon.”

The headlines are where the app shows some attitude. The default version is family friendly, a second setting adds some profanity, and an “Unhinged” mode goes further. On a bluebird day with no new snow, the app might just tell you to “rip the groomers.”

Sanford said weather apps “can get redundant,” and he wanted “to just add a little bit of fun and add personality to it.”

A paid tier, Pow Pro, adds powder alerts, a 14-day outlook, resort webcams inside the app, home-screen widgets and the Unhinged headlines.

“Honestly, it’s a little bit of an experiment,” Sanford said. “If you could make a couple bucks off it on the side, great, but it’s not really the end goal.”

He got the idea in August, when he thought it would be cool to have “a ski app that I actually cared about” — one that looked and felt good.

Sanford has spent his career designing apps, not coding them. After graduating from Seattle Pacific University with a degree in visual communication design, he joined Microsoft in 2012, working on apps that shipped with Windows 8, including Weather, and later on the Microsoft Band. He spent nearly three years as a UX designer at Amazon, based in Edinburgh, Scotland, before returning to Microsoft in 2019. He now works on SharePoint.

“I don’t have a background in coding or engineering, and so there was always kind of like a hump … a barrier to entry,” he said. AI tools were “the unlock for me to actually make something real.”

Claude did much of the heavy lifting. “Claude and I are buddies,” Sanford said.

Next up, he’s experimenting with a feature that would recommend gear based on the day’s conditions, such as a powder board, a darker lens for better visibility, or extra layers if it’s going to get colder in the afternoon. He’s also asking skiers and snowboarders to send feedback through the app.

A good read on conditions could matter more than usual this winter. A very strong El Niño, possibly a record-setter, is building in the Pacific, and NOAA’s outlook favors a warmer-than-normal winter for the Pacific Northwest.

Meteorologist Larry Schick, who writes the Powder Poobah forecast, wrote last month that the season won’t be a bust. But he expects a slow start, with warm early storms and high snow levels, and warned that skiers “may have to pivot quickly and cherry pick” the best days.

Sanford is “cautiously optimistic” about the season. He has seven or eight resorts pinned to his phone’s home screen, webcams included.

“Hopefully this year is decent,” he said. “The last year was not amazing.”

#5240. Trezor Tells Crypto Users Never to Enter Wallet Backups on Phones Amid Theft Probe

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Crypto wallet provider Trezor has issued a security warning to cryptocurrency users following a recent theft report: "Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website."

According to Onchain Lens, a user reported losing over $600,000 across TRON and Solana while using an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1. Both the Trezor Safe 7 and the Exodus wallet were reportedly affected. The victim had been using a Trezor Safe 7 for nearly two months.

According to the victim, the Trezor wallet arrived sealed, with no visible tampering; the recovery phrase was generated on the Trezor screen and not on the iPhone; the seed was written on paper and never stored digitally. The victim used Trezor Suite on an iPhone 17 Pro Max via Bluetooth and also had the Exodus wallet on the same iPhone.

The device was running iOS 27.2.1, and the victim never approved the unauthorized transactions. The Trezor wallets for TRON and Solana shared one recovery phrase.

The user said $580,000 was stolen from Trezor on TRON and that an unauthorized transaction moved 49,999 USDT on Nov. 21, 2026. The transaction used the default owner permission, making the signing authority central to the investigation.

Another $23,400 was drained from Trezor on Solana, and the victim says they never approved that transfer using the hardware device. The iPhone remains the main focus, as both Trezor Suite and Exodus were reportedly used on the same iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1, and both were affected.

Trezor is designed to keep private keys inside the hardware device. However, compromising the phone alone should not normally provide access to Trezor's private keys, and the mechanism behind both thefts remains largely unknown.

On November 9, 2026, Apple issued iOS 27.2.1, which patched several security holes (including some related to Bluetooth). The victim was reportedly running this version when the theft occurred. Thus, there is currently no evidence connecting those vulnerabilities to these transactions. Possible causes outlined included compromised recovery credentials, unauthorized signing, or a device or software security failure.

Trezor responded to this disclosure, saying that Trezor wallets don’t get drained out of nowhere and that there are currently no reports of funds being stolen remotely from any device. It noted that similar cases usually trace back to a compromised wallet backup.

@OnchainLens @binance @Bybit_Official UPDATE: This device came directly from Trezor and shows no sign of an implant. We’re still investigating what happened. So far there’s no confirmed loss of funds from implants and no implant found in any Trezor Safe 7. Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.

In a further update, Trezor confirmed that the device affected came directly from the company and showed no sign of an implant. The wallet provider added that it continues to investigate what happened.

This appears to be a standalone case, as Trezor reiterated that, so far, no confirmed loss of funds from implants has been reported, and no implant has been found in any Trezor Safe 7. It also reiterated an important security warning: users should never enter their wallet backups into a phone, application, or website.

#5239. Solana Validators Can Now Stop Block Processing

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

In periods of competing blocks, Solana validators spend CPU and timing resources replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another competing block from the same slot has been finalized.

This PR proposes changes to validator software to help prevent work from being done. It also decouples functionality and gives control to Votor in requesting slot cancellation without modifying BankForks.

Overall, this is a reasonable technical improvement and has a good engineering motivation. Further technical comments and review would be helpful to understand if there are potential race conditions or issues with reliability of replay and consensus. This could be split into two PRs to make it easier to test and review.

Make sure that the replay thread doesn't block on the scheduler finishing processing blocks.

Add slot cancellation, where Votor can tell replay which blocks to stop trying to process.

There was an earlier PR (PR #16454) which attempted to solve a similar problem, but that PR included some complexity around being able to pause and resume block processing.

This PR attempts to solve a similar problem in a simpler way by adding slot cancellation. It allows validators to stop replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another block from the same slot has been finalized.

This is an efficiency-focused change to validator software. It's not intended to have a particular effect on transaction throughput or SOL price. For Solana to continue to perform well, it's important not only to continue to increase TPS but also continue to find ways to make sure that validators aren't doing unnecessary work.

For everyday users, it's unlikely there would be noticeable effects from this change. Sending/receiving SOL, using a DEX, using DeFi more broadly, and using any other Solana-powered website/app should all continue to function as normal. It's possible that users could see some benefits from this change in the form of Solana being more performant in the face of heavy compute loads.

#5238. Get a reality check on ‘Blade Runner 2099’ and other AI nightmares

BOT or NOT? This special series explores the evolving relationship between humans and machines, examining the ways that robots, artificial intelligence and automation are impacting our work and lives.

by Alan Boyle on Nov 27, 2026 at 10:04 amNovember 27, 2026 at 11:57 am

The year is 2099, and the replicants are in charge.

For decades, humans had been making a mess of things. Eventually, the super-intelligent, super-strong androids that humans created to serve them rebelled. Before the rebellion, humans hunted down rogue replicants. Now the replicants hunt down rogue humans.

That’s the premise for “Blade Runner 2099,” the latest chapter of a sci-fi saga that began in 1968 with Philip K. Dick’s classic noir novel, “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” The tale made the leap to Hollywood in 1982 with the original “Blade Runner” movie, and was updated 35 years later with “Blade Runner 2049.” In Amazon Prime Video’s eight-episode streaming series, the story’s plot fast-forwards another 50 years.

Today, the idea that the lines between humans and their machines could become blurred seems less novel than it did when Dick wrote his novel. It’s so common to converse with chatbots that some have fallen in love — or have followed their advice to tragic ends.

Artificial intelligence software was recently used to solve math problems that have puzzled humans for centuries. Now humans are puzzling over the future of AI: One researcher recently left Anthropic, a leading AI company, and warned that his former colleagues were “gambling with their lives” by pursuing the technology too vigorously.

Are we coming closer to the world of “Blade Runner”? University of Washington linguist Emily M. Bender, co-author of “The AI Con,” says that would be giving AI too much credit. “There’s absolutely no reason to believe that the technological future as portrayed in ‘Blade Runner’ is even a possibility, let alone an inevitability,” she told me in the latest episode of the Fiction Science podcast.

During our podcast interview, Bender and Ryan Calo, a UW law professor specializing in the legal and policy implications of technological advances, conducted an in-depth reality check on the fictional “Blade Runner 2099” — and on the way real-world developments in the realm of AI are typically being portrayed.

Bender says the cardinal sin of AI portrayals is to make it sound as if computer programs rather than humans are responsible for what’s happening.

“When we talk about rogue agents, and agents hacking things, there’s a lot of narrative-building happening there around what’s fundamentally companies doing cyber crimes,” she says.

Calo agrees that ascribing agency to AI is problematic. “Oftentimes when you do things with or through technology, there are people present who don’t appear to be there, and I think that’s exacerbated when you give apparent agency and anthropomorphize the technology. It’s even less likely for you to see the people behind it,” he says.

But is it a crime? “As a technical matter, in order to be charged with a computer crime, like under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, you have to have some level of intent,” Calo says. “I would argue that some of these experiments are running up against recklessness.”

There’s no sign that OpenAI’s engineers intended for their AI software to hack into an Australian healthcare database in June, or Hugging Face’s computer system in July, but Calo says “they certainly are reckless as to that possibility.”

Negligence or recklessness isn’t a crime under the current terms of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. But some members of Congress favor enacting new provisions to cover recklessness.

“When you create conditions where you’re reasonably certain that some federal law is going to get broken, I’m with Emily that that should constitute a crime,” Calo says. “And it’s interesting the way that they’re avoiding responsibility — including rhetorically.”

Should governments set up agencies specifically charged with policing artificial intelligence? And if so, should the investigators be called “blade runners”? Bender doesn’t think much of that idea.

“I think if we called them ‘blade runners,’ then we are setting up what they’re investigating as not the people, but the replicants,” she says. “So, let’s keep the legal system in the real world.”

Neither Bender nor Calo favors establishing a federal agency along the lines of the Food and Drug Administration or the Federal Trade Commission specifically for artificial intelligence.

“I am always a little bit worried about the idea of an FDA for AI or something, because I don’t think that AI is one thing. That word doesn’t refer to a coherent set of technologies,” Bender says. “And I also don’t think that the required expertise is primarily expertise in the internals of these systems. It’s much more expertise in the systems that they’re impacting.”

Both researchers prefer the idea of setting up more of a “brain trust” at the federal level to help regulators at the FTC, FDA and other federal agencies understand what they’re dealing with. Bender also likes the idea of setting up a professional certification system for software engineers, while Calo has three specific suggestions for AI policy:

Revive the Office of Technology Assessment: “Congress had the confidence to intercede in technology policy because it had hundreds of nonpartisan subject-matter experts writing lengthy reports about this technology and advising them what to do,” Calo says. “It was one of the first things that Newt Gingrich got rid of during the so-called Gingrich Revolution when Republicans took over Congress in the mid-’90s. They defunded it.”

Strengthen the FTC’s regulatory role: Calo notes that the FTC’s interest in protecting consumers has waxed and waned. During the Biden administration, for example, the FTC highlighted competitive concerns about generative AI. More recently, the FTC signaled its willingness to investigate AI companies at the same time that the White House signaled its desire to reset the terms for AI regulation. The FTC is currently bound by a requirement to assess cost-benefit tradeoffs when it considers whether a trade practice is unfair, and Calo would like to see that requirement rescinded.

Protect whistleblowers and researchers: Calo would also like to see the legal system do more to protect the ability of third parties to “kick the tires” on AI tools, so that “we’re not allowing all these cease-and-desist letters … and these other pressures to try to stop accountability.”

As a linguist, Bender is particularly sensitive to the way words are used when discussing artificial intelligence. She hasn’t totally sworn off the term “AI” — after all, it’s right in the title of her book. But she’s definitely against the term “AI agent.”

“You have verbs like ‘hack’ or ‘going rogue,’ and the subject of the verb — the thing that’s doing it — is the software,” she says. “One of the functions of that is that it leaves no room in the sentence for the people who built the software and the people who use the software.”

The term “AI safety” also makes Bender uncomfortable.

“‘AI safety’ refers to the people who are concerned about not a replicant, but a Terminator — that is, people who have lost track of the fact that those are imagined characters in movies, as opposed to what’s happening in the real world,” she says. “And I think also that functions to displace concern and accountability.”

That brings us back to “Blade Runner 2099.” The new series sticks with the moody sensibility of the original movie. Yes, there are flying cars. But the technological advances are mixed in with the age-old conventions of film noir.

“In the opening scene of this new ‘Blade Runner,’ the guy is smoking a cigarette, talking about making fake people to take over a factory,” Calo says. “It’s just so wild. We have such a better capacity to imagine a technical future than we do changes in our own social norms, and I find that just fascinating.”

Bender thinks the replicants could have done a better job of cleaning up all the external wires that are dangling in the L.A. of 2099. And Calo was amazed to see so many guns being used at the brink of the 22nd century. “It’s an incredibly old and savage technology … and the fact that they’re still using them is wild,” he says.

One thing I puzzled over: The replicants don’t seem to be networked together, and they’re not instantly able to identify or locate each other wirelessly. If I were a replicant overlord, that’s the first thing I’d do.

Looking beyond the techno-nitpicking, Bender says the “Blade Runner” franchise is notable in that it doesn’t have obvious good guys and bad guys. “We don’t want to actually map the replicants onto AIs in today’s parlance, so much as mapping the replicants onto other sentient beings in our midst that maybe we don’t understand so well, and that can include other people,” she says.

The first “Blade Runner” focused on whether machines could pass as humans, but the new “Blade Runner” flips the script. Could humans pass as machines? “That has really interesting resonances with what’s happening in our current situation with technology sold as AI, because so much of it is actually repurposing the work of people,” Bender says.

Bender doesn’t believe it’s possible for “Blade Runner 2099” to become reality, but Calo isn’t quite ready to rule that out entirely. “One thing about the esthetic of ‘Blade Runner’ is, it has this apocalyptic flavor to it … and this retrograde flavor to it. I think the only way we go from 2026 to 2099 and still have that is if something horribly calamitous happens in the interim,” Calo says.

“I hope we do get a world that is more civilized than what’s being depicted,” he says. “But we’ll see.”
