#5237. XRP Ledger Posts 370% Payment Spike After Sharp Price Rebound

Although XRP has begun to cool from the sudden price recovery witnessed at the beginning of the week that allowed it to reclaim the $1 price level, payment activity across its network has remained high.

After multiple days of extreme caution from traders, the latest on-chain data from XRPScan shows a sharp resurgence in payment volume on the XRP Ledger.

The data shows that the total volume of XRP transferred between accounts on the XRP Ledger surpassed a massive 997.2 million XRP on November 23rd.

Further data shows that this marks an increase of about 370.1% in XRP payment volume over the last 24 hours; this means that the amount of XRP transferred between accounts has soared significantly after the major drop in activity seen the previous day.

The rapid spike in volume has drawn attention as it far exceeds the network's 30-day average payment volume of 791.8 million XRP.

While the surge has coincided with a sharp rebound in the price of XRP, it appears that transaction activity has picked up considerably as the market regains confidence.

It is important to note that the surge in XRP payment volume has come after XRP witnessed a parabolic price move, showing a daily increase of over 10% after reclaiming its $1 price level.

However, it appears that the rally has cooled as XRP has briefly fallen back into the red, retesting $0.9 once again.

Although its price movement has become weak again, on-chain data shows that its network activity remains strong as holders continue to move the token across accounts.

#5236. Companies want AI-ready workers. Are they willing to adapt, too?

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 27, 2026 at 1:00 pmNovember 27, 2026 at 11:48 am

Companies want workers who can adapt to AI. Arif Gursel has a question for those employers: Are they willing to change, too?

Preparing people for technological change cannot fall entirely on students, universities or employees trying to keep their skills relevant, said Gursel, a serial entrepreneur who runs training programs in coding, AI and other fields.

“A skilled and adaptable workforce also needs a skilled and adaptable workplace. Those things have to be in balance,” he said, speaking at a recent Technology Alliance event focused on building talent in Washington state.

A study released Monday by the Schultz Family Foundation points to a related disconnect. Based on nearly 3,000 interviews with young adults, employers and others, it found that 79% of Washington businesses want new entry-level workers to have mid-level AI skills or better. Slightly less than half of the young adults surveyed felt their schooling cleared that bar.

The study didn’t examine whether employers are changing how they train workers. It did find that more than 80% of employers are interested in internships, apprenticeships and similar programs, but 77% say they lack the staff time to make that happen.

Gursel said the challenge extends to experienced workers, too. He called on employers to help design training, connect it to actual jobs and make the workplace somewhere people can develop new capabilities, rather than simply replacing those whose skills no longer match the task.

He offered an example from a past coding training program he helped build with Microsoft, a company where he worked for more than a decade early in his career. Gursel, founder of the corporate strategy firm 8genC, partnered with a Microsoft hiring manager and together they developed a curriculum and the manager committed two open positions to graduates.

Gursel argued that AI tools present an opportunity to build those kinds of partnerships again, with companies helping community colleges and nonprofits prepare people for work rather than leaving educators to guess what employers will need.

Ingrid Stegemoeller, of the Washington Roundtable’s Partnership for Learning, echoed some of those ideas in a statement about the Schultz family study.

“If we make it simpler for employers to share clear signals about the jobs and skills they need with schools, colleges and training programs, we can turn their participation into coursework and work-based learning that prepare young people for those jobs,” she said.

Coleman Bryant, a technology innovation master’s candidate at the University of Washington, also spoke on the panel. He raised concerns about AI and education: Students, he said, can end up “offloading all of the critical thinking to the AI” instead of working out solutions on their own.

He called for hands-on, interdisciplinary education that requires people to connect technical knowledge with business, design and collaboration.

The study indicated schools may be sending mixed signals on AI. About as many young adults said their institution discouraged AI use (36%) as said it helped them learn to use it (34%).

There’s also the fundamental issue of access to AI tools, Gursel said.

“There are underserved and under-resourced and marginalized communities all across Washington state, especially as we think about our tribal communities, our indigenous communities, our Black and Brown communities,” he said.

“How do we build the bridge for that digital divide that is just widening as a result of AI?” he asked.

#5235. Amazon discriminated against Iranian job candidate under global hiring policy, Ontario tribunal rules

by Todd Bishop on Nov 27, 2026 at 2:21 pmNovember 27, 2026 at 2:21 pm

An Ontario human rights tribunal ruled that Amazon violated provincial law when it dropped a Toronto software engineer from its hiring process because of his Iranian citizenship.

The company’s internal policy, applied worldwide, barred some Iranian citizens from jobs involving access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, according to the ruling.

In a Nov. 16 decision, the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario ordered Amazon to pay 15,000 Canadian dollars (about US$10,500) plus interest to Mohammadhasan Owlia, whose hiring process it ended in 2020. The tribunal rejected Amazon’s argument that U.S. export controls required the policy.

Export controls are U.S. rules that limit who can get access to certain American technology, including some encryption software.

The tribunal found that Amazon never showed that the mid-level software engineering job for which Owlia applied would have involved any restricted technology. Expert witnesses for both sides agreed that the U.S. rules don’t ban hiring Iranian citizens, though a company may need a government license before giving them access to certain technology.

“Stated simply, Amazon’s export controls compliance policy was overbroad,” wrote Cyndee Todgham Cherniak, the tribunal vice-chair who decided the case.

Amazon said in a statement to Canadian news outlets that it is committed to “fair and inclusive hiring and to following the laws wherever we operate, including Ontario’s Human Rights Code,” and that it will review the decision and meet its obligations under it.

The ruling was reported earlier by the Toronto Star and the Globe and Mail. We’ve asked Amazon whether the policy remains in effect elsewhere, including in the U.S.

Owlia, a University of Toronto engineering graduate who held an open work permit allowing him to work in Canada, applied for the job in 2019 and passed Amazon’s online technical assessment. On a pre-interview call in January 2020, a recruiter noticed he had studied in Tehran and told him Amazon had a policy against hiring Iranians.

Amazon’s guide for recruiters, quoted in the decision, says to end the process in those cases and tell candidates only that the company “has decided to not move forward with the hiring process.”

The policy, as quoted in the decision, also covers citizens of Cuba, North Korea, Sudan and Syria. It covers candidates, employees, temporary workers and contractors with access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, except lower-level warehouse jobs. It applies globally, but it exempts U.S. citizens, U.S. permanent residents, refugees, people granted asylum, and anyone whose most recent citizenship or permanent residency is from a country not on the list.

Owlia’s lawyers noted that an Amazon recruitment manager acknowledged during cross-examination that the policy remained in effect, according to the ruling. She also testified that Owlia would have been eligible once he became a Canadian permanent resident in 2021.

The tribunal’s orders apply only to hiring in Ontario by Amazon Fulfillment Services ULC, the Canadian subsidiary named in the case. Within six months, Amazon must revise the policy and the recruiter guide to require compliance with Ontario’s Human Rights Code there, and its Ontario-based HR staff must take human rights training.

The tribunal declined to award about C$92,500 (about US$65,000) in lost wages, calling the claim too speculative.

“In my view, having to comply with multiple laws is a cost of doing business,” Todgham Cherniak wrote.

In the U.S., the Immigration and Nationality Act protects U.S. citizens and nationals, eligible permanent residents, refugees and people granted asylum from hiring discrimination based on citizenship status. Workers on temporary visas generally fall outside that specific protection. The Justice Department has warned employers that screening out applicants from particular countries can still amount to national origin discrimination.

The U.S. Commerce Department says that giving Iranian nationals access to controlled technology or certain software can require a license, including when the transfer happens in the U.S. or a third country.

A similar dispute surfaced at Booking.com in 2022, when the company canceled the employment contracts of 11 Iranian hires living in Iran just before they were due to start at its Amsterdam headquarters. Booking.com cited complications in hiring and relocating them and said the move had nothing to do with discrimination, Skift reported. An internal document cited a possible “sanction risk” in employing Iranian residents, according to NL Times.

“I’m proud that I stood up for my right to be judged on my ability to do the work, instead of where my birth certificate was issued,” Owlia said in a statement released by his lawyers at Toronto firm Kastner Ko.

Owlia is now a Canadian citizen and an engineering manager at a Toronto software startup.

#5234. Bitcoin, XRP Hit by $875 Million Squeeze After Nvidia Euphoria Fades: Main Crypto News This Morning

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

On Tuesday morning, the crypto market gave back almost all of the gains it made after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO on Monday. According to CoinMarketCap data, the price of Bitcoin stood at around $60,000 on Tuesday morning, and on Monday evening, Bitcoin was trading as high as $64,372. XRP was back at $0.93 on Tuesday morning after the cryptocurrency reached $1.026 on Monday.

The price of Ethereum was between $1,680 and $1,695 on Tuesday morning, according to CoinMarketCap. In addition, the Crypto Fear and Greed Index stood at 10 on Tuesday, and the index showed extreme fear in the market.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had $569.7 million in net outflows on Monday, Nov. 23, SoSoValue data shows. Spot XRP ETFs in the U.S. also saw outflows on Monday, and the total amount of these outflows was $2.5 million.

On Monday, Nvidia's board voted to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO after input from senior levels of the U.S. government, according to the company's press release. Nvidia shares closed 31.5% higher at $165.05, and the company added $954.3 billion in market value in one session. That is more than twice the previous one-day record of $450 billion that Microsoft set in July.

The S&P 500 gained 4.73% on Monday, and the Nasdaq 100 gained 6.86%. Bitcoin followed the rally and rose to $64,372 on Monday evening, and XRP reached $1.026.

Nvidia shares were down 4.1% at $158.03 in premarket trading on Tuesday, and Nasdaq 100 futures lost 1.62% on Tuesday morning. The VIX rose 8.72% to 28.93 at the same time.

Anthropic shares traded below the $83 IPO price on Tuesday. Earlier, all seven co-founders of the AI company filed to sell a combined $1.96 billion worth of Anthropic stock, or about $280 million each, and there was also news about internal safety problems at Anthropic.

According to CoinGlass data, 146,356 traders were liquidated over the past 24 hours, and the total amount of liquidations reached $875 million.

Short sellers were hit first during Monday's rally, and short positions accounted for $473 million of the total. The largest single liquidation was a $17.83 million BTC-USD position on Hyperliquid. On Tuesday morning, it was the turn of long positions. Over the past 12 hours, longs accounted for $168.85 million out of $207.37 million in liquidations.

Bitcoin dropped as low as $59,366 and was trading at around $60,300 on Tuesday morning, down 1.5% over 24 hours. Bitcoin liquidations amounted to $372.68 million. In addition, open interest in Bitcoin futures rose 1.31% to $39.49 billion as the price was going down.

XRP followed Bitcoin and fell from $1.026 to $0.9238 before it stabilized at around $0.93. XRP liquidations reached $14.05 million over 24 hours, and 3,350 traders were affected. The Coinbase premium for XRP was -0.13%, and the premium for XRP in South Korea was 1.56%.

BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes also commented on the Nvidia rally. According to Hayes, Nvidia's rise is the worst-case scenario for crypto portfolios. Hayes said that crypto needs a crash in U.S. stocks that would force the Fed to start printing money again.

The U.S. Department of Justice has filed a forfeiture complaint against more than $1.1 billion in USDC stablecoins. The funds were stolen from Binance by North Korean hackers on Oct. 29, and Circle helped the authorities with the case. According to the Department of Justice, North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance in the attack. Earlier in November, the department said that U.S. authorities and private companies had frozen more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds.

The Ethereum Foundation also addressed the threat of artificial intelligence. According to the foundation, AI is a more urgent threat to the network than quantum computers. In a blog post, the EF developers said that AI finds vulnerabilities in code faster than auditors can check them, and they also said that AI could break mathematical algorithms that have been used for decades.

EF researcher Justin Drake also spoke about Ethereum's move to hash-based cryptography at Devcon 8 in Mumbai. Drake said that he hoped to complete the transition by December 2028. Earlier, the Ethereum Foundation set December 2029 as the deadline for quantum resistance in its roadmap.

There was other news from regulators and banks as well:

According to Grayscale, the current bear market for Bitcoin has lasted 411 days, and it is the longest one in history. Still, Grayscale called it the mildest one. Bitcoin fell 56% from its October 2025 peak of $124,824 to last week's low of $55,254, according to Grayscale.

Galaxy Research put the drawdown at 53%. According to Galaxy, Bitcoin lost 85%, 84% and 77% in the bear markets of 2013–2015, 2017–2018 and 2021–2022, respectively.

The market capitalization of altcoins excluding Bitcoin and Ethereum dropped to $630.71 billion on Tuesday.

According to CoinGlass data, large buy orders for Bitcoin on OKX and Binance were placed between $59,137 and $59,366 on Tuesday, and $30.3 million worth of long positions could be liquidated in the same range. A large sell order for Bitcoin was placed on Hyperliquid at $60,682, and $64.4 million worth of short positions could be liquidated near $63,996.

The max pain price for Bitcoin options expiring on Nov. 25 stood at $61,000, and the notional value of these options was $642.3 million.

For XRP, liquidations data shows a buy order on Gate at $0.9240 and $577,200 worth of long positions that could be liquidated at $0.9187. Sell orders for XRP on Gate and Hyperliquid were placed between $0.9340 and $0.9444, and $1.4 million worth of short positions could be liquidated at $0.9887.

Two-year U.S. inflation swaps fell to 2.09% ahead of the PCE report, the lowest level for the swaps since September 2024.

#5233. Defying the industry slump, a video game veteran and his son launch ski resort sim ‘Powder Park’

by Thomas Wilde on Nov 28, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 28, 2026 at 8:01 am

2026 has been the latest in a series of bad years for the video game industry. Despite the current success of Grand Theft Auto 6, it came out after months of studio closures, canceled projects, dried-up funding, and multiple waves of layoffs. This was the year when we had to confront the idea that a crash was not just coming, but was already here.

It’s hard to imagine a worse environment in which to start a studio, let alone release a video game. Even so, that’s the backstory behind the recent release Powder Park: Ski Resort Builder.

Developed in Woodinville, Wash., Powder Park began as a collaboration between retired game developer Patrick Wilkinson and his son Maverick.

In Powder Park, built with the Unreal Engine, players build and manage both a virtual ski resort and the mountain it’s on, including all of its skiing courses. You can freely reshape the local terrain, then go ski or snowboard down your own custom tracks. In addition, you can play Powder Park by yourself or cooperatively with friends via Steam, whether you’re in a downhill race or teaming up to build the resort.

The senior Wilkinson is a veteran of the games industry. He retired in 2025 after almost 30 years as a co-founder and studio head at Cat Daddy Games in Kirkland. (The studio’s name is a borrowed term from the timber industry, used to refer to people who climb cut trees to untangle them from other trees’ branches.)

Patrick co-founded Cat Daddy in 1996 with Harley Howe and Ryan Haveson, after nearly four years as a software engineer in Microsoft’s early games group, where he worked on titles including Microsoft Flight Simulator, Microsoft Golf and the Windows Entertainment Packs. At Cat Daddy, which was acquired by Take-Two Interactive in 2003, Patrick co-developed games like the Ski Resort Tycoon series, the Carnival Games franchise for the Nintendo Wii, and WWE Supercard on mobile.

“I was going to retire and just start getting back into my hardware projects,” Patrick told GeekWire. “Then my son graduated with his game degree [in 2025] and all the game jobs dried up. There was nobody in his graduating class by that December who had a game job.”

Given current industry conditions, the Wilkinsons opted to start The Cat’s Eye Studio in Woodinville. The game combines Maverick’s programming (he borrowed the snowboarding physics from a parkour action game he’d made as a senior project) with Patrick’s experience on Ski Resort Tycoon at Cat Daddy.

“How could I say no?” Patrick said. “There are all these resources at my fingertips. I’d hate myself if I walked away. I’ve got somebody who really wants to build a game, he has friends, and I know people who were laid off that are just begging to work. Let’s do a game.”

Development on Powder Park started in December 2025. By the time of its release earlier this month, the Cat’s Eye Studio team had grown to 12, which includes several recent graduates, a college student, and some professional developers who’d recently gotten laid off. Patrick has funded the project out of pocket.

“There’s no downside, really, aside from the financial risk and the time investment, of course,” Patrick said. “For me, it doesn’t have to make money. I’m retired enough that I don’t have to make money.”

He continued, “So being able to do a game effectively for fun, that’s an excellent experience for my son. He learns Unreal. He sees what it takes to do a game from start to finish, and it’s a lot, and when to reach out for help, because we started with just the two of us.”

The resulting game is a spiritual sequel to Ski Resort Tycoon. You can build an entire town for your ski resort, complete with rides and attractions, then drop down into it and explore it at ground level. In addition to skiing or snowboarding down user-created courses, you can get on your park’s Ferris wheel, use its skating rink, or fire yourself or your friends out of a cannon.

“It felt strange that you would have a game that’s about building a ski resort, that you can actually ski and snowboard in, and then not have the tools to bring other people into it to enjoy it with you,” Maverick said. “That’s a big community aspect that we try to push.”

Powder Park: Ski Resort Builder is currently available for PC on Steam for $19.99. Cat’s Eye Studio’s plan for Powder Park is to continue to support it with post-launch content for the foreseeable future.

#5232. Binance to Temporarily Suspend All Crypto Withdrawals on November 25: Reason

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

In a new announcement, Binance crypto exchange said it will perform wallet maintenance on November 25, 2026 at 06:00 (UTC). To support the wallet maintenance, Binance stated that withdrawals for all networks will be suspended beginning on November 25, 2026 at 06:00 (UTC). The recovery is estimated to take about 60 minutes.

The trading of tokens on Binance will not be impacted during the wallet maintenance. The exchange did not announce a corresponding suspension of deposits in the notice. Thus, the temporary suspension specifically concerns withdrawals across all networks.

In its notice, Binance said that withdrawal services will be resumed when the network is deemed to be stable and that no further announcement may be made.

Those looking to transfer funds should make their withdrawals before the wallet maintenance is set to begin to avoid delays and possible loss of funds.

Wallet maintenance refers to a standard operational process that supports blockchain updates, system improvements, and fund security.

This comes weeks after Binance suffered an historic hack with $6.3 billion in assets affected. Binance has since completed coverage of assets impacted in the security incident and published a new Proof of Reserves snapshot.

In a recent development, Binance stated it has engaged leading security firms Mandiant, SlowMist and Verichains for independent reviews of its security procedures.

These reviews, the exchange said, will validate its current security infrastructure, assess its security posture going forward, and help strengthen the protections expected from the crypto platform.

Binance also stated that it was coordinating closely with the U.S. Department of Justice, as well as with industry partners who have assisted in freezing assets impacted by the security incident in late October 2026.  The collaboration is necessary throughout the asset forfeiture process, with the goal of supporting the return of affected funds as efficiently as possible.

In separate news, Binance said it has integrated the Cboe Global Indices Feed into its platform, app and Binance AI, giving users access to real-time traditional market data. The initial rollout covers three of the world's most widely followed U.S. equity benchmarks, with more benchmark data to follow: S&P 500 Index, Dow Jones Industrial Average, Nasdaq-100.

Mark Hurd, who until last month was one of two CEOs leading the database software giant Oracle, passed away this morning at age 62, one month after telling employees in a letter that he was taking a leave of absence owing to health reasons. TechCrunch has more here.

SoftBank Group is assembling a rescue financing plan for WeWork that may value the office-sharing company below $8 billion, according to Bloomberg. The new figure is a fraction of the $47 billion valuation the startup commanded as recently as January, and yet it *still* seems a little high when compared with its bigger, profitable, publicly traded rival IWG, whose valuation is roughy half that amount.

Fun fact: Amazon went public in 1997 with $16 million in revenue and a market cap of $438 million. #ThoseWereTheDays. EquityZen allows accredited investors to access proven pre-IPO tech firms like Impossible Foods, SpaceX, Stripe, Rivian Automotive and Epic Games through its pooled funds. Explore EquityZen’s secondary market today.

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

Madbox, a 4.5-year-old, France-based mobile games studio, has raised $16.5 million in Series A funding from Alven. TechCrunch has more here.

Tenfold, a four-year-old, Austin, Tex.-based maker of customer service software, has raised $7.5 million in Series C funding led by Next Coast Ventures, with participation from earlier backers Andreessen Horowitz, Geekdom Fund, and Salesforce Ventures. Pulse 2.0 has more here.

Bloomberg Beta, the six-year-old, San Francisco-based outfit that uses Bloomberg LP’s money to make bets on startups, has closed its third fund with $75 million, according to Roy Bahat, who’d previously run the online media company IGN and who operates the fund as an equal partnership with Karin Klein and James Chan. (Klein formerly ran Bloomberg’s new initiatives; Chan was formerly a principal with Trinity Ventures.) We talked with Bahat briefly last night about the new vehicle to ask how its capital will be deployed.

The Kik messaging platform has been bought by MediaLab, a holding company which operates Whisper and a number of other apps, the company announced earlier today. CoinDesk has more here.

Eisnor reported to Adam Neumann and had “hired a group of designers, researchers and engineers focused on urban problems such as housing affordability and constructing buildings with sustainable material,” says the outlet, adding that her team of about 30 employees have left the company or are planning to depart.

#5230. Ripple’s $2.8 Billion Stablecoin Flips Telegram’s Gram After $1 Breakdown

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Ripple's U.S. dollar stablecoin Ripple USD (RLUSD) has overtaken Gram (GRAM), the token previously known as Toncoin, in the CoinMarketCap ranking of cryptocurrencies by market capitalization.

According to CoinMarketCap data, RLUSD had a market capitalization of $2.82 billion on Tuesday and ranked No. 26, and Gram dropped to No. 27 with a market capitalization of $2.79 billion.

Gram fell below $1 and was trading at around $0.97 on Tuesday, down about 6% over the past seven days, according to CoinMarketCap. The 24-hour trading volume of Gram stood at around $47 million, and RLUSD had about $368 million in trading volume over the same period.

World Liberty Financial USD (USD1) also had a market capitalization of $2.82 billion on Tuesday and was one spot higher, at No. 25. Among stablecoins, Tether (USDT) and USDC still lead the list with $174.64 billion and $69.22 billion, respectively.

In late July, the market value of RLUSD was about $1.5 billion, according to RWA.xyz data. On Aug. 25, Ripple said that RLUSD had crossed $2 billion in market capitalization, with close to $1 billion of the supply issued on the XRP Ledger. By mid-September, RLUSD supply stood at $2.44 billion.

In late October, the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave Ripple approval for Ripple National Trust Bank. A day later, on Oct. 27, Moody's Ratings assigned RLUSD an A2 long-term deposit rating and a P-1 short-term deposit rating. RLUSD is issued by Ripple subsidiary Standard Custody & Trust Company. Also in late October, RLUSD became available on Coinbase and Robinhood.

The Open Network renamed its token from Toncoin to Gram in June 2026. On July 21, Telegram founder Pavel Durov announced a native non-custodial Gram wallet for every Telegram app. "This summer will see the largest rollout of a non-custodial crypto wallet in human history. Instant zero-fee crypto transactions for over a billion users are about to become reality," Durov wrote.

This week, Telegram published the terms of service for Gram Wallet. According to the terms, the wallet is operated by RAZOR UNIVERSAL CORP., a Panamanian company, and Telegram provides the apps through which users access it. "Telegram does not operate Gram Wallet, does not hold your keys or assets, and is not a party to these Terms," the document says.

The terms also say that "neither we nor Telegram can freeze, seize, move, recover or reverse your assets." At the same time, according to the terms, "anyone who visits your Telegram profile may be able to see your associated Gram Wallet address," as well as the total balance of the wallet. Access to the wallet "may be restricted or unavailable in certain regions or to certain users," the document says.

XRP has completed a short-term golden cross against Bitcoin, giving bulls a fresh technical signal as the cryptocurrency eyes a retest of $1.

The 50 MA rose above the 200 MA on the 3-hour chart, completing a golden cross, as XRP saw relative outperformance against Bitcoin. The timing of the golden cross remains surprising given the current selling in the market.

At the time of writing, XRP was down 5.83% in the last 24 hours to $0.923, giving back most of a rally that sharply took it past $1 after Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia.

On Monday, Nvidia shocked the markets with the surprise announcement of Jensen Huang returning as the CEO of the popular tech and AI company. For crypto traders, the initial response looked extremely encouraging as most tokens sharply rose. However, the rebound began fading, with most cryptocurrencies seeing visible losses in an ongoing selloff in the early Tuesday session.

Bitcoin was down 5.23% in the last 24 hours to $60,298, with total liquidations across the crypto market reaching $596 million.

The $1 price point remains significant for XRP as it is slightly above the lower boundary of the channel in which XRP traded in recent months.

XRP failed to break above the $1.55 resistance at the top of the channel and completed a full reversal toward the channel’s lower boundary at $0.99. XRP broke below this key support level in the past week, cascading to a low of $0.86, last seen in November 2024.

This drop also coincided with a death cross on the daily chart of its USD pairing, the first such occurrence in 2026. For the bearish outlook to weaken, XRP would need to reclaim $0.99 as support.

XRP's attempt to return above $1 has met a brick wall since mid-November. On November 18, XRP's price rise stopped exactly at $1, before it started to decline again.

On November 23, 2026, XRP tried to break above $1 again after reaching $1.02, but bulls could not hold the momentum. If the price goes above $1, XRP will target $1.21 and $1.40. On the downside, key support is expected near $0.80 and $0.64.

#5226. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

Blueground, a six-year-old, New York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. WestCap Investment Partners and Prime Ventures co-led the round. More here.

Databricks, a six-year-old, San Francisco-based SaaS business that’s built on top of a bunch of open source tools, has raised a massive $400 million in Series F funding at a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion valuation. Today’s funding brings the total raised to almost a $900 million. Andreessen Horowitz led the round with new investors BlackRock,  T. Rowe Price Associates, and Tiger Global Management also participating. TechCrunch has more here.

IonQ, a four-year-old, College Park, Md.-based startup that uses charged particles suspended in a vacuum, as the basis for its hardware, has raised $55 million in funding. Samsung and Mubadala Capital co-led the round, joined by Amazon, GV, and New Enterprise Associates. Fortune has more here.

Aurora Insight, a three-year-old, Washington, D.C.-based startup that provides a “dynamic” global map of wireless connectivity that it built and monitors in real time using AI combined with data from sensors on satellites, vehicles, buildings, aircraft and other objects, has raised $18 million in Series A funding. Alsop Louie Partners and True Ventures co-led the round,  joined by Tippet Venture Partners, Rise of the Rest Seed Fund, Promus Ventures, Alumni Ventures Group, ValueStream Ventures, and Intellectus Partners. TechCrunch has more here.

Benevity, an 11-year-old, Calgary, Alberta-based company that makes corporate social responsibility and employee engagement software, has raised $30.5 million in Series C funding from General Atlantic and JMI Equity. More here. EV Connect, a 10-year-old, L.A.-based company that sells software to manage electric vehicle charging, has raised $12 million in a Series B round led by Mitsui & Co. and Ecosystem Integrity Fund. The company has raised $25 million to date. TechCrunch has more here.

Octave, a year-old, San Francisco-based tech-based behavioral health practice, has raised $11 million in Series A funding led by Greycroft, with participation from Obvious Ventures and earlier backers. The company has raised at least $14 million to date. Crunchbase News has more here.Signal AI, a six-year-old, London-based business intelligence and media monitoring startup, has raised $25 million in Series C funding. Redline Capital led the round, joined by MMC Ventures, GMG Ventures, and Hearst Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

AllWork, a 3.5-year-old, New York-based on-demand work platform that’s targeting large enterprise customers in need of temporary workers, has raised $3.8 million in seed funding from Great Oaks, Lightspeed Scout Fund, The Fund, Fernbrook, SmartHub, and numerous angel investors. More here.

Beem, a year-old, Boston-based CBD company that’s marketing its branded oils, protein bars, and a salve to athletes who may be looking for alternatives to chemically derived pain relievers and anti-inflammatories, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by Obvious Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Intrepida Bio, a newly launched, San Diego-based biotech focused on modulating innate immune systems, has raised $9.5 million from Sofinnova and Canaan Partners. FierceBiotech has more here.

LabGenius, a seven-year-old, London-based startup that’s applying AI and robotic automation to protein drug discovery, has raised $10 million in Series A funding. The round was led by Lux Capital and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Felicis Ventures, Inovia Capital, Air Street Capital and earlier investors, along with numerous notable individuals. TechCrunch has more here.

Margin Edge, a four-year-old, Falls Church, Va.-based maker of restaurant management software, has raised $5 million in Series A funding led by Osage Venture Partners, with participation from Good Company. More here.

Medinas, a two-year-old, Berkeley, Ca.-based company that helps healthcare organizations resell their surplus medical equipment and supplies, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by NFX. Additional investors in the round include Precursor Ventures, Sound Ventures, FJ Labs and Bryan Frist (of HCA Healthcare’s founding family). Crunchbase News has more here.

MediView XR, a two-year-old, Cleveland, Oh.-based medical device company working on a surgical navigation system that leverages augmented reality and spatial computing to provide surgeons with advanced visualization, has raised $4.5 million in seed funding. Backers include Inside View Investment,Plug and Play Ventures and Northwest Ohio Tech Fund. More here.

Reibus, a year-old, Atlanta, Ga.-based online marketplace for industrial materials, has raised $3.25 million in seed funding led by Bowery Capital, with participation from Initialized Capital and Stage 2 Capital. More here.

Marcelo Claure, the chief operating officer of SoftBank Group, will assume the position of executive chairman of the board of directors of WeWork when the company receives a planned $1.5 billion payment from SoftBank. TechCrunch has more here.

John Donahoe, the current president and CEO of ServiceNow, is taking over as the CEO and president of Nike in January, replacing Mark Parker who has been since 2006 and lived through numerous controversies over the years. Donahoe knows Nike well, having joined its board, where he will retain a seat, since 2014. In the meantime, Parker will become the company’s executive chairman and Bill McDermott, who abruptly resigned as the longtime CEO of SAP earlier this month for reasons that weren’t clear, is taking over as CEO of ServiceNow. The company’s shareholders apparently prefer Donahoe, who is also the chairman of PayPal and a former CEO of eBay, which he led from 2008 through 2015. At least, shares of ServiceNow dropped in price on the news.

Zaz Floreani has joined the Austin-based venture firm Next Coast Ventures as a principal. Floreani was most recently the VP of corporate development at the same-day delivery company Dropoff. More here.

Manuel Henriquez, founder and former CEO of Hercules Growth Technology Capital, and his wife Elizabeth have both pleaded guilty for their roles in the college admissions cheating scandal. She is to be sentenced Feb. 7 and her husband on March 5. The San Jose Mercury News has more here.

#5225. Nvidia Stock Jumps 9% Pre-Market as Trump Pushes Huang’s Return: Will the Board Bend?

Nvidia stock (NVDA) rose about 9% in pre-market trading on Monday, November 23, after President Donald Trump urged the company’s board to bring back Jensen Huang. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” Trump wrote on Truth Social late on Sunday.

BREAKING: President Trump says he hopes Nvidia’s board, $NVDA, rehires Jensen Huang.“It would be the best thing for the company and for the USA,” Trump says. pic.twitter.com/sARHIMKFb9

The bounce follows a brutal run. Nvidia closed Friday at $125.53, down 14% in a single day, its worst session since the DeepSeek sell-off in January 2025. It was the stock’s seventh losing week in a row, its longest streak since 2008.

Trump wants Huang back, but the path is far from smooth. Nvidia’s board says it will not reinstate him. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants answers on export controls, and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is reportedly looking at the company’s accounting.

So where does Nvidia stand now, and can Trump’s backing turn the stock around?

Explore: Lagarde Sees a €23 Billion Opportunity: Can Tokenization Finally Unite Europe’s 27 Markets?

Huang resigned as CEO, president, and board member on November 12, the company said in its CEO transition release. Chief financial officer Colette Kress became interim CEO.

He left after admitting to an extramarital affair. US intelligence officials suspect the woman, Alice Huang (no relation), of spying for China. She is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China against US export rules.

Trump has backed Huang ever since. On November 16, he told reporters he “would not mind” a return and said Huang had “learned a big lesson.” On Friday, he said he would love to see Huang “be given a second chance.” Sunday’s post went further.

The board has not moved. Chair Harvey Jones said the board “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Nvidia has hired the search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent chief.

Outside pressure is building anyway. An online petition backing Huang, signed by Elon Musk, has passed 200,000 names.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

The administration does not speak with one voice. On November 15, Bessent called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia and said the board should hire a CEO from outside.

He also asked whether Nvidia staff were “pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings.” He compared the case to a bank, saying regulators “would be in there right now.”

By Sunday, his tone had changed. “I said they should go to the outside, but he’s on the outside now,” Bessent told CBS’s Face the Nation. That left the door open to a return without endorsing one.

The China question has not gone away. Bessent said Nvidia must tell the administration by November 25 whether shell companies were used to get its most advanced chips into China. “Was it at the lower levels? Was it the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top?” he asked.

The selling has nothing to do with demand. On November 17, Nvidia posted third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and well above the $109.1 billion analysts expected. It guided to about $130 billion for the current quarter, assuming no data center sales in China.

“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. The market did not agree. To see how the scandal and the stock lined up, we matched each day’s close since Huang’s affair came out with that day’s news.

Nvidia stock had already slipped 22% from its October 6 record close of $239.24 by November 6, as investors worried about AI spending. Then the scandal hit. Over the next 10 trading sessions, the shares lost another 33%, falling on nine of those days.

The earnings beat bought no relief. From the November 17 close of $155.46, the shares dropped 19% in three sessions, with Friday’s 14% fall driven by the SEC report. Nvidia now trades at about 8.4 times expected earnings, CNBC calculated, against about 29 times for AMD.

At $125.53, Nvidia stock closed at its lowest level since May 2025. It is down 47.5% from the October record, a loss of about $2.7 trillion in market value.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

Nvidia stock trades around $136 before Monday’s open, going by Hyperliquid’s Nvidia perpetual contract, which trades around the clock. It sits well below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $185, and its 200-day EMA at $202.

XYZ:NVDAUSD 1D chart. Source: Hyperliquid

Trump’s support gave the stock a lift, but the board, Bessent’s November 25 deadline, and the SEC will decide what comes next. Until Nvidia answers the China questions, a rebound above $150 looks hard to hold.

#5224. Grayscale Confirms Bitcoin’s Record Bear Market

Although Bitcoin has recently reclaimed the $60,000 price mark after seeing a sudden shift in market sentiments that triggered increases of over 6% in its price during the last day, momentum has slowed again, further stretching the prolonged volatility seen over the past months.

With the Bitcoin bear market still persisting, Grayscale has sparked discussions across the crypto market after drawing attention toward a major bearish milestone for the asset.

Earlier today, Grayscale revealed that Bitcoin's current bear market has lasted more than 411 days and is becoming the longest on record.

While this marks an historic milestone in the Bitcoin bear market, Grayscale further disclosed an interesting twist that makes the current bear market pretty different from previous times.

The source confirmed that this bear market has been relatively mild in terms of price losses despite lasting longer than previous downturns.

All through the current bear market, Bitcoin has only posted a price decrease 56%, suggesting that it has suffered considerably smaller losses than several previous bear markets.

This means that even though Bitcoin has spent more than a year in a bear market, its decline has not been as severe as those seen in earlier cycles.

To back the data, Grayscale showed charts comparing Bitcoin's performance across historical bear markets that ended in June 2011, December 2013, December 2017, November 2021, and the ongoing October 2025 cycle.

While the 2011, 2017 and 2021 bear cycles suffered massive losses, especially during the former when its indexed performance fell below 10, the current 2025 bear market broke historical pattern by enduring a longer period yet a comparatively modest decline in Bitcoin’s price.

#5223. October 23, 2019

That WeWork deal could fall apart yet, suggests a new Bloomberg report that states SoftBank Group will seek approval of its bailout package with the Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S., which has stymied SoftBank before. As the report notes: “SoftBank won approval from the panel to buy Sprint Corp. and U.K. chip designer ARM Holdings. However, the committee put conditions on its ownership of Sprint, and restricted its control of alternative-asset manager Fortress Investment Group. More recently, SoftBank was unable to fill two board seats at one of its portfolio companies, Uber Technologies, because it did not have Cfius approval.”

Tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a new factory in Shanghai. Shares rose more than 20 percent after hours. CNBC has more here.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.)

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the company’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”

Fabric, a four-year-old, New York-based startup that wants to make automated logistics available to retailers of all sizes, has raised $110 million in Series B funding. Corner Ventures led the round, joined by Aleph, CPPIB, Innovation Endeavors, La Maison, Playground Ventures, and Temasek. TechCrunch has more here.

Disperse, a four-year-old, London-based startup whose computer vision-driven construction software aims to identify issues on a site, has raised $15 million in Series A funding led by Northzone. VentureBeat has more here.

#5222. Saylor Spots New Role for Bitcoin

Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor sees new ways to put Bitcoin (BTC) to work on Wall Street.

According to staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Bitcoin can be used to meet certain financial resource requirements for U.S. derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses.

‘Next step for adoption is using Bitcoin to work,’ Saylor wrote on X in response to the CFTC advisory published on Nov. 23.

As per the guidance, these companies must maintain sufficient financial resources to cover their operating costs for at least a year.

As clarified by CFTC staff, Bitcoin and Ether can be used to meet this requirement (as well as payment stablecoins). The advisory also provides guidance on how staff interpret the current rules. It also applies to swap execution facilities (SEFs), which are platforms where counterparties trade swaps.

Bitcoin holdings worth $10 million could count for $8 million toward the annual requirement, based on the minimum 20% discount that CFTC staff said they would accept. This provides some flexibility in case Bitcoin's price falls. The discount is also called a haircut.

For Ether, the same minimum 20% haircut applies. For payment stablecoins, the haircut is 2%.

This provides some incentive for an exchange to actually hold BTC. Exchanges could hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets and use some of its value to satisfy this reserve requirement. There would be no need to sell it for USD first.

However, a futures exchange still needs to have sufficient unencumbered cash or highly liquid securities to cover its operating costs for at least six months. Bitcoin, Ether and even payment stablecoins do not fall into this category.

The same six-month liquidity requirement applies to clearinghouses. Additionally, they need to maintain sufficient financial resources to cover a default by a clearing member.

CFTC staff also noted a potential downside for exchanges holding crypto reserves. During a market slump, there's a risk that an exchange's operating losses might rise. At the same time, the value of the Bitcoin it holds to cover those losses might fall.

So this possibility should be considered before an exchange decides whether to use Bitcoin to meet its financial resource requirements.

#5220. XRP Ledger Volume Per Account Up 437% as Trades Get Bigger

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Each account trading on the XRP Ledger's decentralized exchange moved an average of 4,328 XRP a day in the third quarter of 2026, up 437% from 805 XRP in the same quarter a year earlier, according to a report that XRP treasury company Evernorth released on Tuesday.

According to Evernorth, the average swap on the XRP Ledger reached 35 XRP in the third quarter, up from 19 XRP in the second quarter and under 6 XRP a year earlier. "The growth came from bigger trades, not more of them," the company wrote in the report.

At the same time, the number of accounts trading on the XRP Ledger's order book fell to 1,042 a day in the third quarter of 2026 from 2,027 a day in the third quarter of 2025. The number stood at 1,203 in the fourth quarter of 2025, 1,324 in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,125 in the second quarter, according to the report.

Order-book volume on the XRP Ledger rose to 4.51 million XRP a day in the third quarter from 1.63 million XRP a day a year earlier, Evernorth data shows.

In total, 5.16 million XRP a day was traded on the XRP Ledger's exchange in the third quarter, and the figure was up 96% year over year, according to Evernorth.

Measured in U.S. dollars, exchange volume on the XRP Ledger fell 15% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the report.

Evernorth also compared the XRP Ledger with Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana, Base, Arbitrum, Avalanche and Polygon. Across these seven networks, exchange volume in dollars fell 42% over the same period, the report shows.

XRP was trading at around $0.93 on Tuesday morning after reaching as high as $1.026 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap.

The report also shows that the average balance of Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin on the XRP Ledger reached $937 million in the third quarter of 2026, up from $539 million in the second quarter. By the end of the quarter, the RLUSD balance on the XRP Ledger stood at $1.15 billion, compared with $670 million at the end of the second quarter, and the number of RLUSD holders on the network rose to 67,449 from 45,620.

According to Evernorth, the XRP Ledger's average share of RLUSD reached 48.5% in the third quarter, up from 34% in the second quarter. Still, Ethereum finished the quarter with more RLUSD than the XRP Ledger. Evernorth noted that on Ethereum, RLUSD "can already be lent," and that on the XRP Ledger, "native lending is in validator voting."

As of Nov. 20, the Lending Protocol amendment had 24 of 35 validator votes, according to XRPScan. The amendment needs 29 votes, held for 14 days, to activate.

Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9, and its shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker XRPN on Oct. 12. The company entered the public markets holding approximately 473 million XRP, according to its press release.

Evernorth announced the deal in October 2025, with investments from SBI, Ripple, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

#5219. New Nvidia CEO Is the Old One: Huang Returns, NVDA Soars 35% and Bitcoin Follows

In the end, Nvidia’s board backed down and reinstated Jensen Huang as the “new” Nvidia CEO. The announcement triggered a broad market rebound, sending stocks higher and adding trillions in market value. But skepticism remains high, particularly across the crypto market, where investors are still waiting for signs of a sustained recovery.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, November 23, 11 days after he resigned, and the stock exploded. The new Nvidia CEO is the old one, and investors cheered. Shares jumped from about $136 to as high as $169 in pre-market trading after the 8:55 a.m. ET announcement.

JUST IN: NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO effective immediately.$NVDA surges 17.2% in pre-market trading following the news.View chart: https://t.co/hAyqV7AZ0j pic.twitter.com/Cvqe52DiGV

That peak was 35% above Friday’s close of $125.53. The stock opened near $163 and traded around $160 shortly after, still up 27%. Crypto went along for the ride. Bitcoin (BTC) rose as much as 5% to about $64,100, and Ethereum (ETH) as much as 7%.

The reversal came a day after President Donald Trump urged the board to bring Huang back. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday.

So how much of the scandal sell-off has Nvidia won back, and what comes next?

Nvidia’s board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang” after meetings with him, it said in its announcement. It said it was satisfied with his “candor and ability to lead.”

It is a sharp turn. On November 17, chair Harvey Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and had hired a search firm for a new Nvidia CEO.

The government helped change that. The board said it heard from “senior levels of the United States government” before deciding. Based on that input, it is confident Huang’s return “poses no national security risk.” Huang resigned on November 12 after admitting an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects of spying for China.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA,” Huang said. “I can’t wait to get back to work.”

Colette Kress, who ran the company as interim CEO, stays on as finance chief. The board’s independent investigation into the foreign intelligence effort will continue, and Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with government inquiries.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

To measure how much the new Nvidia CEO news repaired, we compared Monday’s price with Nvidia’s closes before and during the scandal.

Nvidia closed at $186.64 on November 6, the last session before Huang’s affair came out. By Friday it was down to $125.53, a loss of $61.11 a share. At $160, the stock has recovered 56% of that drop. At the $169 peak, it had won back 71%.

The peak took it above its close on November 12, the day Huang resigned ($166.19). Even at $160, the jump adds about $830 billion to Nvidia’s market value in a single morning.

The stock is still far from its highs. It sits 33% below its October 6 record close of $239.24, because it had already fallen 22% on AI spending worries before the scandal began.

Bitcoin’s move shows how closely crypto now trades with Nvidia. BTC jumped from about $61,100 to above $63,000 in the same minutes as NVDA, and crypto stocks such as Strategy (MSTR) also rose.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

Nvidia stock trades around $160, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $186, and its 200-day EMA at $202.

XYZ:NVDAUSD 1D chart. Source: Hyperliquid

What comes next depends on Washington more than the boardroom. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants answers from Nvidia by November 25 on whether its chips reached China through shell companies. A reported SEC look at its accounting is still open. Huang is also due to testify to Congress in December.

With the new Nvidia CEO back in charge, those answers will decide whether the stock can hold above $150.

#5218. October 25, 2019

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.]

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”

Note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity plans, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a new book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

It’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz says creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this new book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

It’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

[Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that says [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

As with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the company. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

And he was making everybody so much money. And the company was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’

To me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

#5217. $9 Billion Wealth Manager Discloses XRP ETF Stake

Atlanta-based investment adviser Arkadios Wealth Advisors, with $8.79 billion in client assets, has disclosed a holding in an XRP exchange-traded fund (ETF) in its most recent quarterly filing, according to BankXRP.

The firm joins a growing list of known XRP fund holders, including Bank of America, National Bank of Canada, and trading firm Susquehanna International Group.

Arkadios submitted its Form 13F filing to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Nov. 23. The filing showed securities worth roughly $7.38 billion across 1,880 holdings as of Sept. 30.

Another regulatory filing shows $8.79 billion in total assets under management.

However, the Nov. 24 post from BankXRP does not reveal the XRP fund's name, the number of shares held or the dollar value of the investment.

Susquehanna reported one of the largest increases in holdings of the Bitwise XRP ETF during the quarter.

The trading firm held 878,786 shares valued at $14.6 million as of Sept. 30, compared to 53,116 shares at the end of June.

Susquehanna added 825,670 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF, making it one of the fund's bigger reported holders.

The next-largest reported holding was Goldman Sachs, with 2.31 million shares worth $38.4 million.

Susquehanna also increased its holdings in the Franklin XRP ETF by adding 399,571 shares. This brought its total to 421,700 shares worth $6.82 million.

The firm also reported 199,374 shares in the Grayscale XRP fund, worth $5.74 million.

Susquehanna's combined holdings in Bitwise, Franklin and Grayscale XRP products were valued at around $27.2 million at the end of the quarter.

National Bank of Canada also appeared in the filings, but with a much smaller position. It held 330 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF, worth roughly $5,500 as of Sept. 30.

The Bitwise fund holds XRP directly. This means investors can gain exposure to the token through a security they can buy in their brokerage accounts.

Two other investment managers reported holdings in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF, which trades under the ticker XRPI.

The fund uses futures contracts to gain exposure to XRP's price movements.

EP Wealth Advisors increased its XRPI holdings by 4,975 shares during the third quarter, a 37% increase from the previous quarter.

The firm held 18,400 shares as of Sept. 30, valued at $147,936.

Bank of America reported a holding of 13,260 shares of the same ETF, worth roughly $106,600.

#5216. October 28, 2019

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it announced two years ago.

Rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is currently hosting a summit where Case announced the new fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

Certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

ACV Auctions, a five-year-old, Buffalo, N.Y.-based online platform for franchise and used-car dealerships to buy and sell wholesale inventory through 20-minute auctions, is reportedly looking to raise $150 million in Series E funding at a post-money valuation north of $1 billion. Reuters has more here.

#5215. LINK, AAVE and UNI Now Supported by Fidelity

Fidelity Investments now supports three new cryptocurrencies on its retail crypto trading platform: Chainlink (LINK), Aave (AAVE) and Uniswap (UNI).

The firm expanded from five available cryptocurrencies to eight on Nov. 24. In just one day, Fidelity added the same number of digital assets that it had added in the four years since it first made Bitcoin and Ether available for customer trading.

Eligible U.S. customers can trade these three tokens on the Fidelity website and app. Some states may have limited access to Fidelity's services.

Fidelity's three new listings include tokens that represent different areas of decentralized finance. Aave is a lending protocol where users can deposit crypto assets to earn interest or use them as collateral for loans. AAVE token holders can vote on changes to the protocol's lending markets and other aspects of its operation.

Uniswap is a decentralized trading platform where users can trade different tokens using shared pools of assets provided by other users. UNI is the Uniswap governance token.

Chainlink provides the data that blockchain apps need to operate. For example, a lending protocol might use a Chainlink price feed to assess the value of collateral for a borrower's loan. Chainlink (LINK) tokens are used to pay for services provided on its network.

Fidelity Crypto started accepting customers from its waitlist in November 2022. At the time, the only two cryptocurrencies it offered were Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH). By March 2023, Fidelity was offering its service to more eligible U.S. investors, but these were still the only cryptocurrencies it allowed customers to trade.

On July 17, 2024, Fidelity added Litecoin (LTC) to its list of cryptocurrencies, bringing the total to three. Over a year later, on Oct. 23, 2025, the company introduced Solana (SOL). In addition to individual retail accounts, Solana became available for crypto IRAs, wealth managers and institutional clients.

Fidelity added its fifth cryptocurrency on Feb. 4, 2026, when it launched Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD) as its first stablecoin available to retail and institutional investors. Eligible users can exchange or redeem each FIDD token for $1. Fidelity waives its usual crypto trading fee when users exchange FIDD for dollars.

#5214. October 29, 2019

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he says that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

The now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the company has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

#5213. Anthropic Stock Trails the SpaceX IPO: ANT Up 6% in Three Days vs SPCX’s 57%
